chapters.title: DCF valuation, step by step

cards.title: A business is worth its future cash
cards.body: A discounted cash flow (DCF) says: a company is worth the **cash it will generate for all its investors, discounted back to today** at a rate that reflects risk. Not last year's profit, not the hype — future free cash. Everything else (multiples, comps) is a shortcut to this idea.

cards.title: Free cash flow to the firm
cards.body: **FCFF = EBIT × (1 − tax) + D&A − Capex − Δ Working capital.** Start from operating profit after tax (NOPAT), add back non-cash depreciation, subtract the cash reinvested in machines and in inventory/receivables. FCFF is cash available to **both** lenders and shareholders, so it is discounted at WACC.

cards.title: WACC — the discount rate
cards.body: **WACC = (E/V) × Ke + (D/V) × Kd × (1 − t).** Ke usually comes from CAPM: **Ke = Rf + β × (equity risk premium)**. Debt is cheaper because lenders take less risk and interest is tax-deductible. Use market values and a target capital structure, not book values.

cards.title: Terminal value
cards.body: Forecast 5–10 years explicitly, then capture everything after with a terminal value. Gordon growth: **TV = FCFF(n+1) ÷ (WACC − g)**. The growth rate g must be below the long-run growth of the economy, and WACC must exceed g, or the formula explodes.

cards.title: Worked: FCFF in year 1
cards.body: EBIT ₹100 cr, tax 25% → NOPAT ₹75 cr. Add D&A ₹20 cr, subtract capex ₹30 cr and a ₹5 cr rise in working capital. **FCFF = 75 + 20 − 30 − 5 = ₹60 cr.** Assume it grows 10% a year for five years: 60, 66, 72.6, 79.9, 87.8.

cards.title: Worked: from EV to price per share
cards.body: At WACC 12%, the five FCFFs are worth ₹258 cr today. TV at year 5 with g = 5%: 87.8 × 1.05 ÷ 0.07 = ₹1,318 cr, worth ₹748 cr today. **EV ≈ ₹1,006 cr.** Subtract net debt ₹200 cr → equity ₹806 cr. With 10 crore shares: **≈ ₹80.6 per share.**

cards.title: Read the sensitivity, not the point
cards.body: About three-quarters of that value came from the terminal value. So a DCF is really a bet on long-run growth and WACC. Always show a **sensitivity table** (WACC ± 1%, g ± 1%) — the range is more honest than one precise-looking number.

cards.q: FCFF is best described as cash available to…
options: All capital providers — debt and equity
cards.explain: FCFF is before any payments to lenders or shareholders, which is why it is discounted at WACC. Cash to equity only is FCFE, discounted at the cost of equity.

cards.q: FCFF next year is ₹70 cr, WACC 11%, g 4%. Gordon-growth terminal value today (at the start) is:
Enterprise value is ₹1,000 cr, debt ₹300 cr, cash ₹100 cr, 20 crore shares. Value per share?
cards.explain: Equity = EV − debt + cash = 1,000 − 300 + 100 = ₹800 cr. ₹800 cr ÷ 20 crore shares = ₹40.

notes.p:
A rupee today is worth more than a rupee in five years, and a risky rupee is worth less than a safe one. **Discounted cash flow (DCF)** turns both ideas into arithmetic: forecast the cash a business will throw off, then shrink each year's cash by a discount rate that reflects time and risk. The sum is the **intrinsic value**.

This matters because accounting profit is not cash. A company can report profits while burning cash on inventory, receivables and factories. Investors — whether a mutual fund buying Infosys shares or a PE fund buying a hospital chain — eventually get paid only out of cash. DCF forces you to model that cash honestly.

points: **1. Forecast FCFF** for 5–10 years: revenue growth → margins → EBIT → NOPAT = EBIT × (1 − t) → add D&A → subtract capex and the increase in net working capital.
**2. Estimate WACC**: cost of equity via CAPM (Ke = Rf + β × ERP), post-tax cost of debt Kd × (1 − t), weighted by target market-value weights.
**3. Terminal value** at the end of the forecast: Gordon growth TV = FCFF(n+1) ÷ (WACC − g), or an exit multiple (e.g. 10× EBITDA) as a cross-check.
**4. Discount everything** to today: PV = CF ÷ (1 + WACC)^t. The sum is **enterprise value (EV)** — the value of the operating business.
**5. Bridge to equity**: Equity = EV − debt + cash (− minority interest, − other claims). Divide by **diluted** shares for value per share.

notes.h: Worked example: a mid-sized Indian manufacturer (illustrative)
notes.p:
**Year-1 cash flow.** EBIT ₹100 cr, tax 25% → NOPAT ₹75 cr. D&A ₹20 cr, capex ₹30 cr, increase in working capital ₹5 cr. FCFF = 75 + 20 − 30 − 5 = **₹60 cr**, growing 10% a year: 60.0, 66.0, 72.6, 79.9, 87.8.

**WACC.** Risk-free rate 7% (roughly a 10-year Indian government bond), beta 1.2, equity risk premium 6% → Ke = 7 + 1.2 × 6 = **14.2%**. Pre-tax cost of debt 9% → post-tax 6.75%. With 70% equity and 30% debt: 0.7 × 14.2 + 0.3 × 6.75 = 11.97%, call it **12%**.

**Discounting.** Discount factors at 12% are 0.893, 0.797, 0.712, 0.636, 0.567. Present values: 53.6 + 52.6 + 51.7 + 50.8 + 49.8 = **₹258 cr**.

**Terminal value** with g = 5%: FCFF in year 6 = 87.8 × 1.05 = 92.2; TV = 92.2 ÷ (0.12 − 0.05) = **₹1,318 cr** at end of year 5. Its present value = 1,318 × 0.567 = **₹748 cr**.

**EV** = 258 + 748 = **₹1,006 cr**. Less net debt ₹200 cr → equity ₹806 cr. With 10 crore shares, **intrinsic value ≈ ₹80.6 per share**. If the stock trades at ₹60, your model says it is cheap — *if* your assumptions hold.

In the example, **74%** of EV came from the terminal value. This is normal and is the single most important thing to understand about DCF. Change g from 5% to 6% and TV jumps to 93.1 ÷ 0.06 ≈ ₹1,552 cr; change WACC from 12% to 11% and it rises further. A tiny tweak to two inputs can move value by 20–30%.

So good analysts (a) keep g at or below long-run nominal economic growth, (b) make sure the business has reached a 'steady state' by the final forecast year — margins and reinvestment stable, and (c) check that the implied exit multiple (TV ÷ final-year EBITDA) looks sensible against peers.

points: **Mismatched cash flows and rates**: discounting FCFF at the cost of equity, or FCFE at WACC.
**Growth without reinvestment**: assuming 8% perpetual growth with zero net capex. Growth needs investment; Aswath Damodaran's rule of thumb links growth = reinvestment rate × return on capital.
**Book-value weights** in WACC instead of market values.
**Double counting cash**: adding cash back while also counting interest income in EBIT.
**Spurious precision**: '₹80.63 per share'. Present a range from a sensitivity table instead.
**Ignoring dilution**: using basic share count when ESOPs and convertibles exist.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p:
Every investment banking, equity research, PE and corporate-finance interview asks some form of 'Walk me through a DCF.' The winning answer is the five-step structure above in under a minute, followed by 'the key judgement calls are the terminal growth rate and WACC, so I'd show a sensitivity table.' Expect follow-ups: why is FCFF discounted at WACC? What happens to value if beta rises? (Ke and WACC rise, value falls.) How do you value a loss-making startup? (Longer forecast, model the path to steady-state margins, probability-weight scenarios.)

In real jobs, DCFs underpin fairness opinions in mergers, impairment testing under Ind AS 36, project appraisals for a new plant, and buy/sell calls in equity research.

points: Value = present value of future free cash flows, discounted at a rate reflecting risk.
FCFF = EBIT(1 − t) + D&A − Capex − ΔNWC; discount at WACC to get enterprise value.
WACC = E/V·Ke + D/V·Kd(1 − t); Ke = Rf + β × ERP (CAPM).
Terminal value = FCFF(n+1) ÷ (WACC − g); keep g below long-run economic growth.
Equity value = EV − debt + cash; divide by diluted shares.
Terminal value is often 60–80% of EV — always show a WACC/g sensitivity table.
Match cash flows to rates: FCFF ↔ WACC, FCFE ↔ cost of equity.

chapters.title: Relative valuation & multiples

cards.title: Price it like its neighbours
cards.body: Relative valuation asks: **what are similar assets selling for?** A flat is priced per square foot from nearby sales; a company is priced per rupee of earnings or EBITDA from similar companies. It is faster than a DCF and reflects today's market mood — for better and worse.

cards.title: Equity vs enterprise multiples
cards.body: **Equity multiples** (numerator = market cap / price): P/E = price ÷ EPS, P/B = price ÷ book value per share. **Enterprise multiples** (numerator = EV = market cap + debt − cash): EV/EBITDA, EV/Sales. Rule: **match numerator and denominator** — EV pairs with metrics before interest (EBITDA, sales); price pairs with metrics after interest (EPS).

cards.title: Trading comps vs precedent transactions
cards.body: **Trading comparables**: multiples of listed peers today — what a small minority stake is worth. **Precedent transactions**: multiples paid in past acquisitions of similar companies — these include a **control premium**, so they are usually higher. Bankers show both, plus DCF, on a 'football field' chart.

cards.title: Worked: EV/EBITDA comps
cards.body: Target EBITDA ₹500 cr. Peers trade at 10×, 12×, 12×, 13×, 16× — median **12×**. EV = 12 × 500 = ₹6,000 cr. Net debt ₹1,000 cr → equity ₹5,000 cr. With 50 crore shares → **₹100 per share**. Use the median, not the mean: one 16× outlier shouldn't drive the answer.

cards.title: Which multiple when?
cards.body: **P/E** for stable, profitable firms with similar leverage (FMCG, IT services). **EV/EBITDA** when debt levels differ (telecom, cement, steel). **P/B** for banks and NBFCs, where assets are financial and marked near fair value. **EV/Sales** or user-based metrics for loss-making growth firms — with caution.

cards.title: Why a higher multiple?
cards.body: A multiple is a compressed DCF. Higher growth, higher return on capital and lower risk all justify higher multiples. That's why an FMCG leader can trade at 50× earnings while a PSU bank trades at a fraction of that. Always explain **why** a company deserves a premium or discount.

cards.title: Interview tip
cards.body: When asked 'Is this stock cheap at 15× P/E?', answer: 'Cheap relative to what? Peers' growth, ROE and risk, and its own history.' A low multiple can be a **value trap** — the market may be correctly pricing in decline.

cards.q: Which pairing is internally consistent?
options: Price / Sales per share before interest to lenders
cards.explain: EBITDA is earned for all capital providers, so it pairs with enterprise value. Market cap pairs with equity metrics like net income.

cards.q: Precedent-transaction multiples are usually higher than trading comps because they include…
cards.explain: Acquirers pay a premium for control and expected synergies, so deal multiples typically exceed trading multiples.

cards.q: Bank valuation is most commonly anchored on…
cards.explain: For banks, debt is raw material, not financing, so EV metrics don't work. P/B, judged against ROE, is the standard.

notes.p:
An asset is worth roughly what **similar assets** are selling for. A house broker in Pune doesn't build a DCF of rent; she checks recent sale prices per square foot nearby and adjusts for floor, view and age. **Relative valuation** does the same for companies: pick a standardised measure (price per rupee of earnings, EV per rupee of EBITDA), observe it for comparable firms, and apply it to your company.

Its strength is that it is market-based and quick. Its weakness is that if the whole sector is overpriced — think of dot-com stocks in 1999 — comps will happily tell you an overpriced stock is 'fairly valued'.

points: **P/E = share price ÷ EPS** (or market cap ÷ net income). Most quoted. Distorted by one-off gains, different leverage and different tax rates.
**EV/EBITDA**, where EV = market cap + debt + minority interest − cash. Neutral to capital structure, popular in M&A and capital-intensive sectors.
**EV/Sales** for early-stage or loss-making firms. Ignores profitability, so only compare companies with similar margin potential.
**P/B = price ÷ book value per share** for banks, NBFCs and insurers. A justified P/B ≈ (ROE − g) ÷ (Ke − g): a bank earning ROE above its cost of equity deserves P/B above 1.
**PEG = P/E ÷ expected EPS growth (%)**: a rough way to compare growth stocks.
**Sector metrics**: EV per tonne of capacity (cement), EV per subscriber (telecom), price per bed (hospitals).

notes.h: Step by step: building a comps table
notes.p:
1. **Choose peers** that share business model, growth, size, margins and risk — not just the same industry label. Comparing Asian Paints with a small regional paint maker is misleading.
2. **Spread financials**: collect market cap, debt, cash and LTM / forward metrics; clean out one-offs.
3. **Compute multiples** and look at the **median and interquartile range**.
4. **Apply** the chosen range to your company's metric, adjusting for differences in growth and quality.
5. **Bridge** EV to equity and per-share value.

**Worked example (illustrative).** Target EBITDA ₹500 cr, net debt ₹1,000 cr, 50 crore shares, EPS ₹8. Peers' EV/EBITDA: 10, 12, 12, 13, 16 → median 12×, range 11–13×. EV range = ₹5,500–6,500 cr → equity ₹4,500–5,500 cr → **₹90–110 per share**. Peer P/E median 13× → 13 × ₹8 = **₹104**. Two methods agree — good. Recent precedent deals in the sector at 14× EBITDA would imply EV ₹7,000 cr and ₹120 per share — the extra ₹16–20 is roughly the **control premium**.

Dividing the Gordon growth formula by earnings gives a justified P/E ≈ payout ratio × (1 + g) ÷ (Ke − g). So three things drive a multiple: **growth**, **risk** (Ke) and **efficiency of growth** (a high ROE firm needs to retain less to grow, so pays out more). This is why Indian consumer-staples leaders with high ROE and steady growth have long traded at much richer P/Es than cyclical metals companies: the market pays for predictability. When you argue for a premium, argue from these three drivers.

points: **Mixing numerators and denominators** — e.g. market cap / EBITDA, which overstates value for highly indebted companies.
**Lazy peer sets** that ignore differences in growth, margins or geography.
**Mixing time periods** — trailing for one company, forward for another.
**Using the mean** when one outlier distorts it.
**Ignoring cyclicality**: steel P/E looks lowest at the peak of the cycle, exactly when earnings are about to fall.
**Value traps**: a low multiple often reflects real problems — governance, disruption, debt.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Equity research reports in India typically set target prices using a multiple of forward earnings ('we value the stock at 30× FY28E EPS'). Investment bankers present a **football field** chart — 52-week trading range, trading comps, precedent transactions, DCF — when pitching to a client or writing a fairness opinion. Interviewers love 'Why might two companies in the same sector trade at very different P/Es?' (growth, ROE, risk, governance, accounting) and 'Why not use EV/EBITDA for a bank?' (debt is operating raw material for banks).

points: Relative valuation = price an asset off similar assets' multiples.
Equity value pairs with equity metrics (P/E, P/B); EV pairs with pre-interest metrics (EV/EBITDA, EV/Sales).
EV = market cap + debt + minority interest − cash.
Trading comps value a minority stake; precedent transactions include a control premium.
Use median and ranges; choose peers on business model, growth and risk.
Multiples are driven by growth, risk and return on capital.
Banks → P/B vs ROE; cyclicals → be careful with peak-cycle P/E.

chapters.title: Investment banking: IPOs and M&A advisory

cards.title: What investment banks actually do
cards.body: Investment banks help companies **raise capital** and **buy or sell businesses**. Two main divisions: **ECM/DCM** (equity and debt capital markets — IPOs, QIPs, bond issues) and **M&A advisory**. Others sit alongside: sales & trading, research. Bankers earn fees for advice and distribution, not by lending their own balance sheet.

cards.title: Why a company goes public
cards.body: An IPO raises growth capital, lets early investors and founders sell (an **offer for sale**), creates a currency for acquisitions and ESOPs, and builds visibility. The price: disclosure, quarterly scrutiny, listing compliance and pressure from public shareholders.

cards.title: Indian IPO roadmap
cards.body: Appoint **book running lead managers** → due diligence → file the **DRHP** with SEBI → SEBI observations → file the **RHP** with the Registrar of Companies → roadshows → **anchor investors** a day before the issue → price band, bidding → allotment → listing on NSE/BSE. Regulated mainly by SEBI's **ICDR Regulations**.

cards.title: Book building, simply
cards.body: Instead of fixing a price, the bankers announce a **price band** and collect bids. Demand at each price reveals what investors will pay. Allocation is split by category — qualified institutional buyers, non-institutional investors and retail — with retail getting a reserved portion. Heavy oversubscription often means the price was set below what demand would bear.

cards.title: The sell-side M&A process
cards.body: Typical auction: prepare **teaser** and **information memorandum** → NDAs → first-round **non-binding bids** → shortlist → management meetings and data room **due diligence** → **binding bids** → negotiate the share purchase agreement → sign → regulatory approvals (e.g. CCI) → close.

cards.title: Worked: IPO arithmetic
cards.body: A company with 80 crore shares pre-IPO issues 20 crore fresh shares at ₹250. Fresh capital = **₹5,000 cr**. Post-issue shares = 100 crore; market cap at issue price = **₹25,000 cr**; public holds 20%. If promoters also sell 5 crore shares via OFS, that ₹1,250 cr goes to them, not the company.

cards.title: Interview tip
cards.body: 'Why investment banking?' needs a specific answer: you enjoy deal execution, financial modelling and client-facing work under deadlines. Back it with a deal you followed — what the buyer paid, why, and how it was financed.

cards.q: In an Indian IPO, the document filed with SEBI first for its observations is the…
cards.explain: The Draft Red Herring Prospectus goes to SEBI first; the RHP (with price band details to follow) is filed later with the Registrar of Companies.

cards.q: In an offer for sale (OFS) portion of an IPO, the money raised goes to…
cards.explain: In an OFS, existing shareholders sell their shares, so they receive the proceeds. Only a fresh issue brings money into the company.

cards.q: In a sell-side M&A auction, buyers typically do detailed due diligence…
cards.explain: Shortlisted bidders get data-room access and management meetings after first-round bids, then submit binding offers.

notes.p:
An investment bank is a **matchmaker and adviser for capital**. Companies need money (equity or debt) or want to buy, sell or merge businesses; investors want opportunities. Bankers price the deal, prepare documents, find the other side, run the process and manage regulators. They are paid mostly in **fees** — a percentage of IPO proceeds, a success fee on an M&A deal — which is why the job is intense: no deal, no fee.

In India, the main players include domestic houses such as Kotak Mahindra Capital, Axis Capital, ICICI Securities and JM Financial, alongside global banks such as Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, JP Morgan and Citi. Boutique advisers handle many mid-market deals.

points: **Equity capital markets (ECM)**: IPOs, follow-on offers, qualified institutional placements (QIPs), rights issues, block deals.
**Debt capital markets (DCM)**: corporate bonds, commercial paper, loan syndication.
**M&A advisory**: buy-side (help a buyer find and value targets) and sell-side (run an auction for a seller); also fairness opinions and restructuring.
**Sales & trading and research**: sell and make markets in securities for institutional investors; research analysts write stock reports (separated by internal 'Chinese walls' from deal teams).
**Analyst life**: building models, pitch books, comps, CIMs and data rooms — long hours, steep learning.

notes.p:
The legal backbone is SEBI's **Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements (ICDR) Regulations, 2018**, plus the Companies Act. A simplified sequence:

1. **Mandate**: the company appoints **book running lead managers (BRLMs)**, legal counsel, auditors and a registrar.
2. **Due diligence and drafting** of the **Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP)** — business, risks, financials, use of proceeds, promoter details.
3. **SEBI review**: SEBI issues observations; the company responds and updates.
4. **RHP**: filed with the Registrar of Companies; the price band is announced shortly before opening.
5. **Roadshows** to institutional investors; **anchor investors** are allotted shares one working day before the issue opens, with lock-in periods.
6. **Book building**: bids are collected across categories — QIBs, non-institutional investors (NIIs) and retail individual investors — each with prescribed allocation shares.
7. **Pricing, allotment and listing**: SEBI has shortened the timeline so shares list within a few working days of the issue closing (the T+3 framework).

Rules change periodically, so practitioners always check the latest SEBI circulars.

**Illustrative company**: 80 crore shares pre-IPO. Fresh issue of 20 crore shares at ₹250 plus an OFS of 5 crore shares by a PE investor.

Fresh issue proceeds = 20 × 250 = **₹5,000 cr** (to the company, minus issue expenses). OFS proceeds = 5 × 250 = **₹1,250 cr** (to the PE investor). Post-issue shares = 80 + 20 = **100 crore**; market cap at issue price = **₹25,000 cr**. If FY26 net profit is ₹625 cr, EPS = ₹6.25 and the IPO is priced at **40× trailing earnings**. Your job as an analyst: is 40× justified by growth and quality relative to listed peers? A large OFS with little fresh issue tells you the IPO is mainly an **exit** for existing holders, not a growth funding round.

**Sell-side** (most common for bankers): prepare a teaser (anonymous one-pager) and a confidential information memorandum (CIM); approach a curated list of strategic and financial buyers; collect **non-binding indicative bids**; shortlist; open the **virtual data room**, run management presentations; receive **binding bids** with a marked-up share purchase agreement; negotiate price, representations, warranties, indemnities and conditions; sign; get approvals (Competition Commission of India for large deals, sector regulators, shareholders); close.

**Buy-side**: screen targets, value them (DCF, comps, precedents, synergies), structure the offer (cash vs stock, earn-outs), and help with financing. For listed Indian targets, crossing SEBI's **Takeover Code** thresholds can trigger a mandatory open offer to public shareholders.

points: Confusing the bank's **advice** with its **capital** — advisory banks mostly don't fund the deal themselves.
Thinking 'oversubscribed 100×' means the stock will do well long-term. It means demand at the price band was huge; long-term returns depend on fundamentals.
Ignoring **OFS vs fresh issue** — who actually receives the money?
Treating listing-day 'pop' as success for the company: a big pop means the company **left money on the table**.
Forgetting that an M&A process can take 6–12 months and many processes end with no deal.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Expect: 'Walk me through an IPO', 'What is book building?', 'Why might a company prefer a QIP to an IPO?' (already listed, faster, institutional only), 'How would you value a target in a sell-side process?' and 'Pitch me a deal' — pick a real Indian or global transaction, explain the strategic logic, price paid and financing. Analysts and associates spend their days on models, comps, pitch books and diligence trackers; the core skills are accuracy, speed and the ability to explain a deal crisply.

points: IBs help companies raise capital (ECM, DCM) and buy/sell businesses (M&A); they earn fees.
Indian IPO path: BRLMs → DRHP to SEBI → observations → RHP with RoC → anchors → book building → allotment → listing.
Fresh issue money goes to the company; OFS money goes to selling shareholders.
Book building discovers price via bids within a price band; categories are QIB, NII, retail.
Sell-side M&A: teaser → CIM → indicative bids → data room → binding bids → SPA → approvals → close.
Large Indian deals may need CCI approval; listed targets may trigger SEBI Takeover Code open offers.
A big listing pop means the issuer left money on the table.

chapters.title: Mergers & acquisitions: synergies, accretion/dilution and why deals fail

cards.title: Why companies buy companies
cards.body: Good reasons: buy growth or a market faster than building it, acquire technology or talent, gain scale, cut costs, or remove capacity. The test is simple: **is the combined firm worth more than the two apart, by more than the premium paid?** That extra value is **synergy**.

cards.title: Value created for the buyer
cards.body: **Buyer's gain = Synergies − Premium paid − Deal costs.** Premium = price paid − target's standalone value. If you pay a ₹1,000 cr premium for ₹800 cr of realistic synergies, the target's shareholders win and yours lose — even if the deal 'makes strategic sense'.

cards.title: Cost vs revenue synergies
cards.body: **Cost synergies** — closing duplicate offices, plants, procurement savings — are more within management's control and more reliably realised. **Revenue synergies** — cross-selling, new markets — depend on customers and competitors, so they are often overestimated. Experienced boards discount revenue synergies heavily.

cards.title: Accretion / dilution
cards.body: An **accretive** deal raises the buyer's EPS; a **dilutive** one lowers it. Quick rule for all-stock deals: buying a company on a **lower P/E** than your own is accretive. For cash deals, compare the target's earnings yield (1/P/E) with your after-tax cost of debt or lost interest on cash.

cards.title: Worked: all-stock deal
cards.body: Buyer: net income ₹1,000 cr, 100 crore shares, EPS ₹10, price ₹200 (P/E 20). Buys target earning ₹200 cr at P/E 15 = ₹3,000 cr, paid in stock: 3,000 ÷ 200 = 15 crore new shares. New EPS = 1,200 ÷ 115 = **₹10.43 → 4.3% accretive.** Pay P/E 25 (₹5,000 cr) instead → 1,200 ÷ 125 = ₹9.60, **4% dilutive.**

cards.title: Worked: debt-funded
cards.body: Same ₹3,000 cr price, borrowed at 8% pre-tax, 25% tax → after-tax interest ₹180 cr. New net income = 1,000 + 200 − 180 = ₹1,020 cr over the same 100 crore shares → EPS **₹10.20, 2% accretive.** Cheap debt makes many deals look accretive — that alone doesn't make them good.

cards.title: Why most deals disappoint
cards.body: Research over decades suggests a large share of acquisitions fail to create value for the buyer. Usual culprits: **overpaying** in a competitive auction (winner's curse), **CEO hubris**, overestimated synergies, culture clash and slow, distracted **integration**.

cards.q: In an all-stock deal, the buyer (P/E 20) acquires a target at P/E 12, ignoring synergies. The deal is…
cards.explain: Buying earnings that are cheaper than your own (lower P/E) with your own stock raises combined EPS.

cards.q: Which synergies are generally most reliably realised?
cards.explain: Cost synergies are within management's control; revenue synergies depend on customers and competitors.

cards.q: Synergies ₹600 cr, premium paid ₹900 cr, deal costs ₹50 cr. Buyer's value created is…
cards.explain: 600 − 900 − 50 = −₹350 cr. The seller captured more than the entire synergy.

notes.p:
A merger or acquisition is an investment like any other: you pay a price today for future cash flows. It creates value for the buyer only if **the value of the combined company exceeds the sum of the two standalone values by more than the premium and costs paid**. That gap is **synergy**. Most of the difficult questions in M&A — how much to pay, how to finance, how to integrate — come back to this equation.

Note the asymmetry: target shareholders usually gain (they receive the premium, often 20–40% above the undisturbed share price in public deals), while the acquirer's shareholders on average gain little or lose. Being the seller is easier than being the buyer.

notes.h: The framework: sources of synergy and value
points: **Cost synergies**: consolidating plants, distribution, IT and head office; procurement scale; eliminating overlapping roles.
**Revenue synergies**: cross-selling, combined distribution (e.g. pushing the target's products through the buyer's dealer network), pricing power.
**Financial synergies**: tax benefits, lower cost of capital — treat with scepticism.
**Dis-synergies**: customer losses, key talent leaving, integration costs — always subtract these.
**Value created for buyer = PV(synergies) − premium − transaction and integration costs.**

notes.p:
**Buyer**: net income ₹1,000 cr, 100 crore shares, EPS ₹10, share price ₹200 (P/E 20).
**Target**: net income ₹200 cr.

**Case A — all stock at P/E 15.** Price = 15 × 200 = ₹3,000 cr. New shares = 3,000 ÷ 200 = 15 crore. Combined net income = ₹1,200 cr; shares = 115 crore; EPS = **₹10.43** (+4.3%, accretive).

**Case B — all stock at P/E 25.** Price = ₹5,000 cr → 25 crore new shares; EPS = 1,200 ÷ 125 = **₹9.60** (−4%, dilutive).

**Case C — all debt at P/E 15.** Borrow ₹3,000 cr at 8%; after-tax cost = 3,000 × 8% × (1 − 25%) = ₹180 cr. Net income = 1,200 − 180 = ₹1,020 cr; shares unchanged at 100 crore; EPS = **₹10.20** (+2%).

**Breakeven synergies for Case B**: EPS returns to ₹10 when net income = 10 × 125 = ₹1,250 cr, i.e. ₹50 cr of after-tax synergies.

Two lessons. First, EPS accretion is mostly arithmetic about relative P/Es and the cost of financing — it says little about whether value is created. A deal can be accretive and still destroy value if the buyer overpays or adds risk. Second, boards care about accretion anyway because markets watch EPS, so you must be able to compute it in an interview.
Studies across decades — including widely cited work summarised in Harvard Business Review — suggest that a majority of acquisitions fail to deliver their promised value. The recurring causes:
points: **Overpaying**: in an auction, the winner is often the bidder with the most optimistic forecast — the **winner's curse**. Richard Roll's **hubris hypothesis** (1986) argued that overconfident managers overpay.
**Synergy optimism**: revenue synergies assumed without evidence.
**Integration failure**: systems, incentives and cultures don't merge; customers and top talent leave in the confusion.
**Strategic drift**: deals done for size or prestige rather than a clear logic.

**Wrong timing and leverage**: buying at the top of a cycle with heavy debt. Tata Steel's acquisition of Corus in 2007, just before the global financial crisis, is often cited as a case where cycle timing and leverage hurt for years.

**Global contrasts**: AOL–Time Warner (2000) and Daimler–Chrysler (1998) are textbook culture-clash failures; Disney–Pixar (2006) is a commonly cited success, partly because Disney protected Pixar's creative culture.

notes.p: Serial acquirers that succeed tend to have a **clear thesis** (why this target, why now, why us as the best owner), **walk-away discipline** on price, a **integration plan ready on day one** with named owners for each synergy, and honest post-deal reviews. Many follow a 'string of pearls' strategy — frequent small, related acquisitions — rather than rare bet-the-company deals. Hindalco's acquisition of Novelis (2007) was criticised for its price at the time but is often described as having worked out strategically over the long run — a reminder that judging deals takes years.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Classic interview questions: 'Walk me through an accretion/dilution analysis', 'Why would a deal be dilutive even with synergies?', 'Would you pay in cash or stock if your shares were overvalued?' (stock — you're using expensive currency; conversely, sellers should be wary of accepting it). In corporate development and consulting roles, you'll build synergy models, plan integration (the 'first 100 days'), and track synergy capture against the board case.

points: Buyer gains only if synergies exceed premium + costs.
Cost synergies are more reliable than revenue synergies.
All-stock: buying a lower-P/E target is EPS-accretive; higher-P/E is dilutive.
Cash/debt deals: compare the target's earnings yield with your after-tax cost of funds.
Accretive ≠ value-creating.
Failures come from overpaying (winner's curse, hubris), synergy optimism and poor integration.
Good acquirers have a thesis, price discipline and a day-one integration plan.

chapters.title: Private equity & LBOs

cards.title: What private equity does
cards.body: A PE fund raises money from **limited partners** (pension funds, sovereign funds, endowments, family offices) and invests it in private companies for roughly 3–7 years, then exits. The **general partner** runs the fund, typically earning a management fee (often around 2%) plus **carried interest** (often around 20% of profits above a hurdle).

cards.title: The leveraged buyout
cards.body: In an **LBO**, the fund buys a company using a large slice of **debt** secured on the target's own cash flows. The company's cash then pays down that debt. Because equity is a small slice, every rupee of value gain lands disproportionately on the equity — leverage magnifies returns (and losses).

cards.title: Three engines of LBO returns
cards.body: 1) **EBITDA growth** — better operations, pricing, add-on acquisitions. 2) **Debt paydown** — cash flow shrinks debt, so more of EV belongs to equity. 3) **Multiple expansion** — selling at a higher EV/EBITDA than you paid. Good funds underwrite the first two and treat the third as a bonus.

cards.title: MOIC and IRR
cards.body: **MOIC** (multiple on invested capital) = equity value at exit ÷ equity invested. **IRR** = annual return that sets NPV of the cash flows to zero. With one entry and one exit: **IRR = MOIC^(1/years) − 1.** 2× in 5 years ≈ 15%; 3× in 5 years ≈ 25%.

cards.title: Worked: simple LBO
cards.body: Buy at 8× ₹100 cr EBITDA = **₹800 cr EV**, funded with ₹480 cr debt (60%) and **₹320 cr equity**. Over 5 years, EBITDA grows to ₹150 cr and free cash repays ₹250 cr of debt (debt → ₹230 cr). Exit at 8× = ₹1,200 cr. Equity = 1,200 − 230 = **₹970 cr → MOIC 3.0×, IRR ≈ 25%.**

cards.title: What makes a good LBO target
cards.body: Stable, predictable cash flows; low capex needs; strong market position; room for operational improvement; a credible exit route (strategic sale, IPO, secondary sale to another fund); and assets or cash flows lenders are comfortable with. A volatile, cash-hungry startup is a poor LBO candidate.

cards.title: India context
cards.body: Indian PE has historically been dominated by **growth and minority** deals, though control buyouts have become more common. Exits happen via IPOs, strategic sales and secondary sales. When discussing Indian PE, mention promoter-led businesses, governance and exit routes.

cards.q: Equity of ₹200 cr becomes ₹600 cr in 5 years. MOIC and approximate IRR?
Which is NOT one of the three classic sources of LBO returns?
cards.explain: Fees go to the GP; they reduce, not create, investor returns. Returns come from EBITDA growth, deleveraging and multiple expansion.

cards.q: The best LBO candidate is usually a company with…
options: Stable cash flows and low capex
Volatile cash flows and big capex needs
Already heavy debt and falling sales
cards.explain: Lenders need predictable cash to service debt; low capex leaves more cash for paydown.

notes.p:
Private equity buys stakes in companies that are not traded on a stock exchange — or takes listed companies private — aims to make them more valuable over a few years, and then sells. The **leveraged buyout (LBO)** is PE's signature move: buy a mature, cash-generative company largely with borrowed money, use the company's own cash to repay that debt, improve operations, and sell. Think of buying a ₹1 crore flat with ₹20 lakh of your own money and an ₹80 lakh loan that the rent pays off: when you sell, almost all the gain belongs to your ₹20 lakh.

The classic story of the 1980s LBO boom is KKR's 1989 takeover of RJR Nabisco, chronicled in *Barbarians at the Gate* by Bryan Burrough and John Helyar.

notes.h: How a PE fund is structured
points: **Limited partners (LPs)** commit capital; the **general partner (GP)** invests it and draws it down as deals arise.
**Fees**: commonly an annual management fee around 1.5–2% of committed capital, and **carried interest** of about 20% of profits above a **hurdle** (often around 8%). Exact terms vary.
**Fund life** ~10 years: invest in the first ~5, harvest in the rest.
**J-curve**: early returns look negative (fees, unrealised investments), then rise as exits happen.
**Deal types**: buyouts (control), growth equity (minority, little debt), PIPEs (private investment in public equity), distressed/special situations.

notes.p:
**Entry.** A packaged-foods company has EBITDA of ₹100 cr. The fund buys it at **8× EV/EBITDA = ₹800 cr**, funded with **₹480 cr debt** (4.8× EBITDA) and **₹320 cr equity**.

**Hold (5 years).** Better procurement, pricing and distribution lift EBITDA to **₹150 cr**. After interest, taxes and capex, the company generates cumulative free cash flow of ₹250 cr, all used to repay debt: debt falls to **₹230 cr**.

**Exit.** Sold at the same 8× multiple: EV = 8 × 150 = **₹1,200 cr**. Equity = 1,200 − 230 = **₹970 cr**.

**Returns.** MOIC = 970 ÷ 320 = **3.03×**. IRR = 3.03^(1/5) − 1 ≈ **24.8%**.

**Value bridge** (equity grew by ₹650 cr):
EBITDA growth: 50 × 8 = **₹400 cr**
Debt paydown: 480 − 230 = **₹250 cr**
Multiple expansion: 0 (bought and sold at 8×)
Total = ₹650 cr ✓

**Without leverage**, the fund would pay ₹800 cr equity and exit with ₹1,200 cr + ₹250 cr of accumulated cash = ₹1,450 cr → MOIC 1.8×, IRR ≈ 12.6%. Leverage roughly doubled the IRR — and would equally have amplified losses if EBITDA had fallen.

notes.h: Where the real value comes from
notes.p: Early LBOs leaned on financial engineering. Today, with competitive auctions and higher prices, top firms emphasise **operational value creation**: professional management, pricing discipline, working-capital release, procurement, digitisation, and **buy-and-build** strategies (a platform company acquiring smaller add-ons at lower multiples). Governance matters too: PE owners install monthly reporting, sharp KPIs and management equity so that leaders think like owners.

points: **Overleverage**: a downturn plus heavy debt can wipe out equity (covenant breaches, refinancing risk).
**Relying on multiple expansion** — buying at 12× and hoping to sell at 14×. Multiples can just as easily contract.
**Confusing IRR with MOIC**: a quick 1.5× in one year is a 50% IRR but little absolute money; LPs care about both.
**IRR manipulation**: subscription credit lines and early dividend recaps can boost IRR without adding wealth.
**Underestimating people issues**: in Indian promoter-led companies, governance, related-party dealings and founder alignment can make or break a deal.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: PE interviews often include a **paper LBO**: given entry multiple, leverage, growth and exit multiple, compute MOIC and IRR in your head in a few minutes. Memorise: 2× in 3 years ≈ 26%, 2× in 5 years ≈ 15%, 3× in 5 years ≈ 25%, 2.5× in 5 years ≈ 20%. Expect 'What makes a good LBO candidate?', 'Walk me through the value bridge', and 'Pitch me a company you'd buy'. As an associate, you'll build models, run diligence with consultants and lawyers, and later work with portfolio-company management on the value-creation plan.

points: PE: LPs supply capital; GP invests it for fees (~2%) and carry (~20% over a hurdle) — terms vary.
LBO = buying a company mostly with debt that the company's own cash repays.
Returns = EBITDA growth + debt paydown + multiple expansion.
MOIC = exit equity ÷ entry equity; IRR = MOIC^(1/n) − 1 for single in/out flows.
Good targets: stable cash flow, low capex, strong position, clear exit.
Leverage magnifies gains and losses.
Rules of thumb: 2× in 5 years ≈ 15%; 3× in 5 years ≈ 25%.

chapters.title: Venture capital: stages, term sheets and the power law

cards.title: VC is a hits business
cards.body: Venture capital funds young, high-risk companies in exchange for equity. Most investments fail or return little; a few return 50× or more. This **power law** means one great company can return the entire fund. So VCs ask 'Could this be huge?' — not 'Is this safe?'

cards.title: Funding stages
cards.body: **Pre-seed/seed**: idea to early product, from angels, accelerators and seed funds. **Series A**: early product–market fit, scaling a repeatable model. **Series B/C+**: rapid expansion. **Growth/late stage**: near-profitable scale, sometimes pre-IPO. Each round typically sells a meaningful minority stake, often 10–25%.

cards.title: Pre-money and post-money
cards.body: **Post-money = pre-money + new investment.** Investor's stake = investment ÷ post-money. Example: ₹10 cr invested at ₹40 cr pre-money → post ₹50 cr → investor owns **20%**. Price per share = pre-money ÷ pre-money fully diluted shares.

cards.title: Worked: the VC method
cards.body: A startup could reach ₹200 cr revenue in 6 years; similar companies sell at 5× sales → exit ₹1,000 cr. The VC wants 10× → post-money today = ₹100 cr. Expecting future rounds to dilute it to 60% of its stake → justified post-money = **₹60 cr**. Investing ₹10 cr → needs **16.7%** → pre-money ₹50 cr.

cards.title: Term sheet terms that matter
cards.body: **Liquidation preference** (who gets paid first in a sale), **anti-dilution** (protection if a later round is priced lower — broad-based weighted average is the market norm), **pro-rata rights**, **board seats**, **protective provisions** (veto on key decisions), **founder vesting**, **drag-along / tag-along**, **ROFR**.

cards.title: Worked: 1× liquidation preference
cards.body: VC invested ₹20 cr for 20%, 1× non-participating. Company sells for ₹50 cr: VC takes the greater of ₹20 cr or 20% × 50 = ₹10 cr → **₹20 cr**; others share ₹30 cr. Sells for ₹200 cr: 20% = ₹40 cr > ₹20 cr, so VC converts and takes **₹40 cr**. Preferences matter most in modest exits.

cards.title: Valuation is not the only number
cards.body: A high valuation with harsh terms (2× participating preference, full-ratchet anti-dilution) can leave founders with less than a lower valuation on clean terms. Founders should model outcomes at several exit values before signing.

cards.q: ₹15 cr is invested at a ₹60 cr pre-money valuation. The investor owns…
cards.explain: Post-money = 60 + 15 = ₹75 cr. Stake = 15 ÷ 75 = 20%.

cards.q: Why do VCs insist each investment could 'return the fund'?
options: Returns follow a power law, so a few outliers drive almost all gains
Every startup is expected to succeed
cards.explain: Because most investments fail, the fund's returns depend on a handful of huge winners.

cards.q: A VC with ₹10 cr, 1× non-participating preference and 10% ownership; company sells for ₹60 cr. VC receives…
cards.explain: Greater of ₹10 cr (preference) or 10% × 60 = ₹6 cr → ₹10 cr.

notes.p:
Venture capital is money for companies that are too young and too risky for banks or public markets but could become very large. The VC buys a minority stake, adds advice and network, and gets paid only when the company is sold or lists. Because most startups fail, VC economics are governed by the **power law**: returns are concentrated in a tiny number of extraordinary outcomes. Peter Thiel's *Zero to One* popularised this idea for founders; it shapes almost every VC behaviour — from chasing huge markets to supporting aggressive growth.

In India, the ecosystem expanded sharply in the 2010s and early 2020s, with firms such as Peak XV Partners (formerly Sequoia India), Accel, Blume Ventures, Elevation, Lightspeed and Nexus, plus many angel networks and accelerators.

notes.h: Stages and what investors look for
points: **Pre-seed / seed**: team, insight, early signs of demand. Instruments: equity, convertible notes or SAFE-like instruments.
**Series A**: evidence of product–market fit — strong retention, a repeatable acquisition channel, early unit economics.
**Series B / C**: scale the engine; expand to new cities, segments, products.
**Growth / pre-IPO**: path to profitability, governance, audit readiness.
Rough heuristic: each round raises enough for 18–24 months of runway, enough to hit milestones that justify a higher next valuation.

notes.p:
**Pre/post money.** A startup raises ₹10 cr at ₹40 cr pre-money → post-money ₹50 cr → investor owns 10 ÷ 50 = **20%**; founders are diluted from 100% to 80%.

**The VC method.** Expected revenue in year 6: ₹200 cr. Comparable companies are acquired at around 5× revenue → expected exit value **₹1,000 cr**. The fund's target for an early-stage bet: **10×** (because many others will fail). Post-money today = 1,000 ÷ 10 = ₹100 cr. But later rounds will dilute the VC — assume its stake shrinks to 60% of today's level. Adjusted post-money = 100 × 0.6 = **₹60 cr**. To invest ₹10 cr, the VC needs 10 ÷ 60 = **16.7%** today, implying a pre-money of **₹50 cr**.
Check: 16.7% × 0.6 × ₹1,000 cr = ₹100 cr = 10× the ₹10 cr invested ✓.

**Power law in a fund.** A ₹500 cr fund makes 25 investments of ₹20 cr each. If 15 return nothing, 8 return 1× (₹160 cr), and one returns 3× (₹60 cr), the fund still needs a big winner. A single company returning 50× (₹1,000 cr) turns the fund into a ~2.4× fund: (160 + 60 + 1,000) ÷ 500 = 2.44×, before fees and carry.

**Economic terms**: valuation, investment amount, option pool (often required to be created in the pre-money — see the cap tables chapter), **liquidation preference** (1× non-participating is the founder-friendly norm; participating or >1× preferences are tougher), **anti-dilution** (broad-based weighted average is standard; full ratchet is harsh).

**Control terms**: board composition, **protective provisions / affirmative voting rights** (investor veto over new share issues, sale, budget changes), information rights, **founder vesting** (commonly four years with a one-year cliff), **drag-along** (majority can force a sale), **tag-along** (minority can join a sale), **ROFR** (right of first refusal on share transfers).

In India, investors usually hold **compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS)**, and these rights are written into the shareholders' agreement and articles of association.

points: **Optimising only for headline valuation**: a high price can create a painful **down round** later if growth disappoints.
**Ignoring preference stacks**: after several rounds, a modest exit may pay investors and leave founders and employees little.
**Raising too much too early**, which inflates burn and expectations.
**Treating VC as the only path**: many excellent businesses (services, profitable niches) are better funded by revenue, debt or angels — they may not fit the power-law model.
**Misreading VC 'no's**: often it's about fund fit (stage, sector, size), not the business.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: VC-associate interviews ask you to **pitch a startup** you'd back (market size, team, why now, moat, risks), to calculate **ownership and dilution**, and to explain **liquidation preferences**. Founders use the same skills when negotiating rounds. Expect: 'Why would a VC pass on a profitable ₹50 cr revenue business?' (it may not return the fund) and 'What's the difference between pre-money and post-money?'

points: VC returns follow a power law: a few winners make the fund.
Stages: pre-seed/seed → Series A (PMF) → B/C (scale) → growth/pre-IPO.
Post-money = pre-money + investment; stake = investment ÷ post-money.
VC method: exit value ÷ target multiple × retention = justified post-money.
1× non-participating preference: investor gets the greater of its money back or its % share.
Key terms: preference, anti-dilution, pro-rata, board, vetoes, vesting, drag/tag.
Indian VC deals typically use CCPS plus a detailed shareholders' agreement.

chapters.title: Finding problems and ideas worth pursuing

cards.title: Start with a problem, not an idea
cards.body: Great startups usually begin with a **painful, frequent, expensive problem** that someone is already trying to solve badly — with spreadsheets, WhatsApp groups, middlemen or workarounds. If nobody is hacking together a solution today, the pain may not be real enough to pay for.

cards.title: Where good ideas come from
cards.body: Paul Graham's essay 'How to Get Startup Ideas' (2012) argues the best ideas are **noticed, not brainstormed**: live in the future, then build what's missing. Sources: your own job frustrations, a new technology that makes something newly possible (UPI, smartphones, AI), regulation changes, and underserved customers others ignore.

cards.title: Jobs to be done
cards.body: Clayton Christensen's lens: customers **'hire' a product to get a job done** — functional, emotional and social. People don't want a drill, they want a hole (or a shelf, or a tidy home). Define the job and you see competitors you missed — and gaps incumbents ignore.

cards.title: A quick idea scorecard
cards.body: Score each idea on: **pain** (how bad?), **frequency**, **willingness to pay**, **market size**, **why now** (what changed?), **your unfair edge** (insight, access, skill) and **competition**. A big market with no 'why now' usually means someone has already tried and failed.

cards.title: Indian case: Zerodha
cards.body: In 2010, retail stockbroking in India charged percentage-based brokerage and pushed customers to trade more. Nithin Kamath, a trader himself, saw that **flat, low fees** plus good technology could serve self-directed investors better. Insider pain + a cost-structure insight + online trading becoming mainstream = 'why now'.

cards.title: Talk to 20 customers before building
cards.body: Ask about **past behaviour**, not opinions: 'Tell me about the last time this happened. What did you do? What did it cost you?' Rob Fitzpatrick's *The Mom Test* warns that people lie politely about the future ('I'd definitely buy that') but not about the past.

cards.title: Schlep blindness
cards.body: Graham also coined **'schlep blindness'**: founders avoid ideas that involve boring, painful work — payments compliance, logistics, government processes. Those schleps are often moats. Razorpay and many fintechs built businesses precisely on messy plumbing others avoided.

cards.q: Which interview question best follows 'The Mom Test'?
options: Would you buy an app that solves this?
How much would you pay for my idea?
Don't you think this is a great idea?
When did this last happen to you, and what did you do?
cards.explain: Asking about specific past behaviour gives facts; hypothetical questions invite polite lies.

cards.q: In jobs-to-be-done thinking, a commuter buying a morning milkshake 'hires' it mainly to…
options: Make a boring drive more bearable and stay full till lunch
cards.explain: Christensen's milkshake story: the job was a long, dull commute that needed a slow, filling, one-handed snack.

cards.q: A large market where many have tried and failed, with nothing new about technology or regulation, mostly lacks…
cards.explain: Without a change that makes success newly possible, you face the same barriers that defeated predecessors.

notes.p:
Most failed startups did not fail because they built a bad product; they built a good product **nobody needed enough**. Investor surveys of startup post-mortems have repeatedly found 'no market need' among the top reasons for failure. So the first entrepreneurial skill is not coding or pitching — it is **choosing a problem**.

A problem worth pursuing is **painful** (people lose money, time or face), **frequent** (it recurs), **owned** by someone with budget, and **currently solved badly**. The best signal is a workaround: shopkeepers keeping credit records in notebooks (the pain that Khatabook-style apps addressed), restaurants taking phone orders, students forming WhatsApp groups to share notes.

points: **Your own work**: frustrations you saw as an employee or customer — you understand the pain and buyer.
**Technology shifts**: smartphones, cheap data after Jio's 2016 launch, UPI, Aadhaar-based e-KYC, and now generative AI made new businesses possible.
**Regulatory change**: GST (2017) created demand for compliance and invoicing software; account aggregators enabled consent-based data sharing.
**Underserved segments**: Bharat users, small merchants, vernacular speakers, MSMEs.
**Unbundling or rebundling**: take one feature of a big product and do it 10× better, or bundle scattered tools into one.
**Copy with a twist**: a model proven elsewhere adapted to Indian price points, languages and distribution — common, but the adaptation must be real.

notes.p:
**Jobs to be done (Christensen)**: identify the progress the customer is trying to make. In Christensen's famous milkshake example, a fast-food chain discovered many morning milkshakes were 'hired' by commuters to make a long drive less boring and keep them full — competitors were bananas and bagels, not other milkshakes.

**Problem–solution–market scorecard**: rate 1–5 on pain, frequency, willingness to pay, reachable market, why now, founder edge, and competition. Kill ideas scoring low on pain or willingness to pay, however clever.

**Customer discovery (Steve Blank)**: 'Get out of the building.' Your business plan is a set of guesses; customers are the only source of facts. Blank's customer-development process precedes and inspired Eric Ries's lean startup.

An MBA student has two ideas:

**Idea A — an app for college students to split mess bills.** Pain 2 (UPI already makes splitting easy), frequency 4, willingness to pay 1, market 2, why now 1, edge 3, competition 2. **Total 15/35.**

**Idea B — software for small clinics in tier-2 cities to manage appointments and WhatsApp reminders.** Pain 4 (no-shows lose revenue, receptionists overwhelmed), frequency 5, willingness to pay 3 (₹1,000–2,000 a month could be justified if it fills even a few no-show slots), market 4 (tens of thousands of clinics), why now 4 (WhatsApp Business API, ABDM digital health push), edge 3 (her parent runs a clinic), competition 3. **Total 26/35.**

The scorecard doesn't make the decision, but it forces the question: who pays, how much, and why now? Idea B's next step: interview 20 clinic owners about their last no-show week.

points: **Solution in search of a problem**: 'Let's use blockchain/AI for…' before finding a pain.
**Asking for opinions** instead of past behaviour; mistaking compliments for demand.
**Building for yourself** when you're not representative of the market (an IIM student is not a typical Indian consumer).
**Ignoring distribution**: a great product with no cheap way to reach customers dies.
**Fear of competition**: competition often validates a market; the question is your differentiated edge.
**Secrecy**: ideas are cheap; execution and learning speed are the advantage.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: B-school entrepreneurship courses and incubator applications ask for a **problem statement, customer segment, evidence of demand and why now**. Product-management and VC interviews ask 'What problem would you solve?' or 'Evaluate this startup idea.' A crisp answer: who has the pain, how they cope today, why existing options fail, what changed, why you.

points: Start with painful, frequent, paid-for problems; look for existing workarounds.
Ideas come from your own work, tech shifts, regulation, and underserved segments.
Jobs to be done: customers hire products for functional, emotional and social jobs.
Every idea needs a 'why now' and a founder edge.
Mom Test: ask about past behaviour, not hypothetical future purchases.
Schleps can be moats.
Score ideas; kill those weak on pain or willingness to pay.

chapters.title: Lean startup, MVP and product–market fit

cards.title: A startup is a search
cards.body: Steve Blank defines a startup as a temporary organisation **searching for a repeatable, scalable business model**. Big companies execute known models; startups don't yet know who the customer is, what they value or how to reach them. So the job is learning fast and cheaply.

cards.title: Build–Measure–Learn
cards.body: Eric Ries's *The Lean Startup* (2011): turn assumptions into **testable hypotheses**, build the smallest thing that tests them, measure real behaviour, and **learn** whether to persevere or pivot. Speed through this loop is the core advantage of a small team.

cards.title: The MVP is an experiment
cards.body: A **minimum viable product** is the cheapest way to test your riskiest assumption — not a buggy version 1. It can be a landing page, a manual 'concierge' service, a WhatsApp group, a 'Wizard of Oz' front end with humans behind it, or a pre-order. Test **demand** before building scale.

cards.title: MVP cases
cards.body: Dropbox's early explainer video drew sign-ups before the full product existed. Zappos's founder reportedly photographed shoes in stores and bought them only when someone ordered online. Many Indian food and grocery startups began by taking orders on phone or WhatsApp and delivering themselves.

cards.title: Product–market fit
cards.body: Marc Andreessen (2007): PMF means **being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market**. You feel it: customers pull the product, usage grows by word of mouth, servers and support struggle to keep up. Before PMF, nothing else matters; after it, scale.

cards.title: Measuring PMF
cards.body: Signals: **retention curves that flatten** (a stable share of users keep coming back), organic growth and referrals, and the **Sean Ellis test** — if roughly **40% or more** of users would be 'very disappointed' without the product, you are likely near PMF.

cards.title: Pivot or persevere
cards.body: A **pivot** changes one part of the model while keeping the learning: customer segment, problem, channel, revenue model or platform. Slack began as an internal tool at a games company; Instagram narrowed from the check-in app Burbn to photo sharing.

cards.q: The main purpose of an MVP is to…
options: Test the riskiest assumption with minimum effort
cards.explain: An MVP is an experiment designed to produce validated learning cheaply.

cards.q: Under the Sean Ellis test, a common PMF threshold is about what share of users being 'very disappointed' without the product?
cards.explain: Roughly 40% 'very disappointed' is the widely used benchmark.

cards.q: Which retention curve suggests product–market fit?
options: Drops early, then flattens at a stable level
cards.explain: A flattening curve means a core group keeps getting value; a curve trending to zero means users eventually all leave.

notes.p:
Traditional business plans assume you know the customer, the product and the channel, and simply need to execute. Startups don't know any of those. The **lean startup** approach treats every belief as a **hypothesis** and the company as an experiment machine whose output is **validated learning**. It grew out of Steve Blank's customer-development method (*The Four Steps to the Epiphany*) and was popularised by Eric Ries in *The Lean Startup* (2011).

The goal of the early stage is **product–market fit (PMF)**: a product that a specific market wants badly enough that growth begins to pull rather than push. Marc Andreessen's 2007 essay argued PMF is the only thing that matters for a startup's early life.

notes.h: The lean method step by step
points: **1. Write the leap-of-faith assumptions**: the value hypothesis (customers will use and pay) and the growth hypothesis (we can reach them cheaply).
**2. Pick the riskiest assumption** — the one that kills the business if wrong.
**3. Design an MVP** to test it: landing page with a 'pay now' button, concierge service, Wizard-of-Oz prototype, pre-orders, a pilot with three customers.
**4. Define success in advance**: e.g. '30% of visitors join the waitlist' or '5 of 10 pilot clinics renew'.
**5. Measure behaviour**, not opinions. Use **actionable metrics** (cohort retention, conversion), not vanity metrics (downloads, page views).
**6. Decide**: persevere, pivot, or kill.

notes.h: Worked example: an MVP for a tiffin subscription (illustrative)
notes.p:
Hypothesis: working professionals in Bengaluru's tech parks will pay ₹3,000 a month for healthy home-style lunches.

**MVP**: an Instagram page and a Google Form; meals cooked by two home chefs; delivery by the founders on scooters. Cost: under ₹50,000 for a month.

**Results after 4 weeks**: 400 form visits → 80 sign-ups for a free trial week (20%) → 36 paid for the first month (45% of triallists) → 27 renewed for month 2 (**75% retention**). Feedback: price fine; delivery timing critical; menu fatigue in week 3.

**Learning**: demand exists and retention looks promising, but the growth hypothesis (cheap acquisition) is untested beyond the founders' network. Next experiment: test paid Instagram ads with a target CAC under ₹600. The founders built no app, no kitchen and no fleet — and still learnt the most important things.

**Qualitative signs**: customers complain when it breaks, recommend it unprompted, use it more over time; sales cycles shorten.

**Quantitative signs**:
points: **Cohort retention curves** that flatten at a healthy level instead of decaying to zero (the right level varies by category — daily social apps vs annual tax software).

**Sean Ellis test**: around 40%+ of surveyed active users say they'd be 'very disappointed' without the product. Superhuman's Rahul Vohra described using this survey as an engine to improve PMF segment by segment.
**Organic growth share** rising — word of mouth, not just paid ads.
**Improving unit economics** as you learn — CAC stable or falling, LTV rising.

notes.p:
Ries lists pivot types including **zoom-in** (one feature becomes the product — Instagram from Burbn), **customer-segment**, **platform**, **channel** and **business-model** pivots. Slack emerged when Stewart Butterfield's team at Tiny Speck abandoned its game Glitch but kept the internal chat tool.

Common mistakes:
points: Treating MVP as an excuse for a bad product — 'viable' still means it must deliver the core value.
Running 'experiments' without a pre-defined success criterion, so every result looks like success.
Scaling marketing **before** PMF — pouring paid acquisition into a leaky bucket.
Pivoting too often (no learning accumulates) or never (sunk-cost attachment).
Applying lean blindly to areas where safety or regulation demands rigour (medical devices, lending).

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: PM and startup interviews ask: 'How would you test demand for X with ₹1 lakh and two weeks?' Answer with the riskiest assumption, MVP design, success metric and decision rule. Corporate innovation teams (e.g. in banks and FMCG companies) use the same approach for new products. Exams may ask you to define MVP, validated learning, pivot and PMF, and to distinguish vanity from actionable metrics.

points: Startup = search for a repeatable, scalable business model (Blank).
Build–Measure–Learn loop; maximise validated learning per rupee and per week (Ries).
MVP = cheapest test of the riskiest assumption.
Set success criteria before the experiment; track actionable, not vanity, metrics.
PMF: flattening retention, organic pull, ~40% 'very disappointed' (Sean Ellis).
Don't scale acquisition before PMF.
Pivot = change one dimension of the model while keeping learning.

chapters.title: Unit economics: CAC, LTV, payback and contribution margin

cards.title: Does each customer make money?
cards.body: **Unit economics** asks whether a single unit — an order, a customer, a subscription — creates more value than it costs. If each unit loses money, growth multiplies losses. Scale can fix fixed costs; it rarely fixes broken unit economics.

cards.title: Contribution margin
cards.body: **Contribution per unit = revenue − all variable costs of that unit** (product cost, shipping, packaging, payment fees, returns, discounts, delivery). Marketing to acquire the customer is usually counted separately as CAC. Contribution must cover CAC and then fixed costs.

cards.title: CAC, LTV, payback
cards.body: **CAC** = total acquisition spend ÷ new customers acquired. **LTV** (contribution basis) = contribution per period × expected customer lifetime; for subscriptions, ≈ monthly contribution ÷ monthly churn. **Payback** = CAC ÷ monthly contribution. A common heuristic: LTV/CAC ≥ 3, payback under ~12–18 months.

cards.title: Worked: a D2C skincare brand
cards.body: AOV ₹1,000. Product cost ₹500, shipping and packaging ₹120, payment fees ₹20, returns ₹40 → **contribution ₹320/order**. Customers order 3 times on average → LTV ₹960. CAC from ads ₹800 → **LTV/CAC 1.2**. Breakeven only after 2.5 orders. Growth here burns cash.

cards.title: Fixing the D2C brand
cards.body: Raise repeat to 5 orders (subscriptions, better product) → LTV ₹1,600, ratio 2.0. Cut CAC to ₹500 (organic content, referrals, marketplaces) → ratio 3.2. Lift AOV to ₹1,300 via bundles → contribution rises because shipping is mostly fixed per order. **Retention is usually the biggest lever.**

cards.title: Worked: a B2B SaaS tool
cards.body: ₹5,000 per account per month, 80% gross margin → **₹4,000 contribution/month**. Monthly churn 2.5% → average life 1 ÷ 0.025 = 40 months → **LTV ₹1.6 lakh**. CAC ₹60,000 → LTV/CAC **2.7**, payback **15 months**. Halving churn to 1.25% doubles LTV to ₹3.2 lakh.

cards.title: Watch the hidden costs
cards.body: Quick-commerce and food-delivery debates in India often centre on contribution after **discounts, delivery and dark-store costs**. Always ask: is CAC blended (including organic users) or paid-only? Are returns and cancellations in? Is LTV based on revenue or contribution? Each choice can flatter the numbers.

cards.q: Monthly contribution per customer ₹600, monthly churn 5%. Approximate contribution LTV?
CAC ₹9,000, monthly contribution per customer ₹750. CAC payback period?
cards.explain: Payback = 9,000 ÷ 750 = 12 months.

cards.q: Which is the most serious red flag?
options: Fixed costs exceed revenue in year 1
cards.explain: If each order loses money before marketing and overheads, more volume only increases losses.

notes.p:
A business is a collection of units — orders, customers, rides, subscriptions. **Unit economics** examines one unit and asks: after everything it costs to serve and acquire it, does it make money, and how fast do we get our acquisition cost back? It is the bridge between a pitch deck and a profitable company.

India's startup cycle of the 2010s offers a lesson: in the cheap-capital years, many consumer startups grew on discounts and paid acquisition; when funding tightened around 2022, investors shifted sharply toward contribution margins and profitability. Companies with sound unit economics survived the shift much more comfortably.

points: **AOV / ARPU**: average order value or revenue per user per period.
**Gross margin**: revenue minus cost of goods (or hosting and support for software).

**Contribution margin** (often called CM1/CM2/CM3 in Indian startups — definitions vary by company): gross margin minus variable fulfilment costs — shipping, packaging, payment gateway, returns, discounts, last-mile delivery. Some firms also deduct performance marketing to get a CM3.
**CAC** = acquisition spend (ads, sales team, referral bonuses, onboarding) ÷ new customers. Distinguish **paid CAC** from **blended CAC**.
**Retention/churn**: share of customers lost per period. Average lifetime ≈ 1 ÷ churn rate.
**LTV** = contribution per period × lifetime (optionally discounted). Use contribution, not revenue.
**Payback period** = CAC ÷ contribution per period.

notes.p:
**Per order**: AOV ₹1,000 (net of GST). Product cost ₹500 (50% gross margin). Shipping and packaging ₹120. Payment gateway ~2% = ₹20. Returns and RTO (return-to-origin) losses averaged across orders ₹40.
**Contribution per order = 1,000 − 500 − 120 − 20 − 40 = ₹320.**

**Per customer**: 3 orders over two years → LTV = 3 × 320 = **₹960**. CAC from Meta and Google ads = **₹800**. LTV/CAC = **1.2**. After the first order the brand is ₹480 in the hole; it breaks even only after 800 ÷ 320 = **2.5 orders**.

**Levers**:
Retention to 5 orders → LTV ₹1,600 → ratio 2.0.
CAC to ₹500 → ratio 3.2 (with 5 orders).
AOV to ₹1,300 via bundles: product cost ₹650, shipping still ~₹120, fees ₹26, returns ~₹52 → contribution ₹452 — a 41% jump from a 30% rise in AOV, because shipping is largely fixed per order.

An HR software tool sells to small companies at **₹5,000 per account per month**; gross margin 80% (hosting, support) → **₹4,000 monthly contribution**.

Monthly logo churn **2.5%** → average lifetime = 1 ÷ 0.025 = **40 months** → LTV = 4,000 × 40 = **₹1,60,000**.

CAC: the sales and marketing team costs ₹30 lakh a month and wins 50 accounts → **CAC = ₹60,000**. LTV/CAC = 160,000 ÷ 60,000 ≈ **2.7**. Payback = 60,000 ÷ 4,000 = **15 months**.

SaaS investors also watch **net revenue retention (NRR)**: if upsells to existing customers exceed revenue lost to churn and downgrades, NRR exceeds 100% and the existing base grows on its own — a hallmark of the best SaaS businesses.

notes.h: Common mistakes and how managers misuse the numbers
points: **Revenue-based LTV** instead of contribution — inflates LTV several-fold.
**Blended CAC** that counts organic users, hiding rising paid CAC.
**Assuming retention** from one strong early cohort; later cohorts acquired through paid ads usually retain worse.
**Ignoring discounts** as an acquisition cost — a ₹200 first-order coupon is CAC.
**Infinite lifetimes**: with very low early churn, LTV formulas explode; cap lifetimes (e.g. 3–5 years) and discount future cash.
**Averaging away** segments: the average may hide one profitable segment and one disastrous one.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Consulting, PM, VC and startup roles all test this. Typical prompts: 'A D2C brand is growing 100% a year but losing money — what would you look at?' (contribution per order, CAC by channel, cohort retention, payback). 'Compute LTV/CAC from these numbers.' In founder or growth roles, you'll present a monthly **unit economics dashboard** with contribution margins by city, CAC by channel and cohort retention.

points: Contribution = revenue − all variable costs per unit; must be positive.
CAC = acquisition spend ÷ new customers; include discounts and sales costs.
Lifetime ≈ 1 ÷ churn; LTV = contribution per period × lifetime.
Payback = CAC ÷ periodic contribution; heuristic LTV/CAC ≥ 3, payback ≲ 12–18 months.
Retention is usually the biggest lever; AOV helps when fulfilment costs are fixed per order.
Use contribution-based LTV and paid CAC by channel and cohort.
Scale fixes fixed costs, not negative contribution.

chapters.title: Fundraising and cap tables

cards.title: The cap table
cards.body: A **capitalisation table** lists who owns what: founders, ESOP pool, angels, funds — and the instruments (equity shares, preference shares, convertibles). Every financing round **dilutes** existing holders' percentages, but if the valuation rises, their stakes can be worth more.

cards.title: Dilution in one line
cards.body: After a round, each existing holder's new % = old % × (pre-money ÷ post-money). Raise ₹20 cr at ₹80 cr pre → post ₹100 cr → everyone keeps **80%** of their previous percentage; the new investor owns 20%.

cards.title: The ESOP pool shuffle
cards.body: Investors usually require an **ESOP pool** (often around 10%) to be created **before** their money comes in — i.e. inside the pre-money. This means founders alone bear the dilution from the pool. A '₹16 cr pre-money' with a 10% post-money pool is effectively ₹14 cr for the founders.

cards.title: Worked: seed round
cards.body: Founders own 100%. Seed: ₹4 cr at ₹16 cr pre → post ₹20 cr. Investor **20%**; a 10% post-money ESOP pool created in the pre-money; founders **70%**. Founders' effective pre-money: 70% × ₹20 cr = **₹14 cr**.

cards.title: Worked: Series A
cards.body: Raise ₹20 cr at ₹80 cr pre → post ₹100 cr. Series A owns **20%**; everyone else × 0.8: founders 70% → **56%**, ESOP 10% → **8%**, seed 20% → **16%**. Total 100%. Founders' stake fell, but its value rose from ₹14 cr to ₹56 cr on paper.

cards.title: SAFEs and convertible notes
cards.body: A **convertible note** is a loan that converts into equity at the next priced round, usually with a **discount** and/or **valuation cap**. Y Combinator's **SAFE** is a simpler right to future equity with no interest or maturity. In India, startups commonly use structures such as **CCPS** and convertible notes permitted for recognised startups, with India-specific variants of SAFE-style instruments.

cards.title: Raise when you don't need to
cards.body: Fundraising often takes 3–6 months. Start with 9–12 months of runway left, aim for milestones that justify the next round, and remember: a lower valuation with clean terms often beats a higher one with harsh terms.

cards.q: Founders own 60% before a round that raises ₹25 cr at ₹75 cr pre-money. After the round they own…
If an investor insists the ESOP pool be created in the pre-money, who bears the pool's dilution?
options: Everyone equally, including the new investor
cards.explain: Creating the pool before the investment means the new investor's percentage is unaffected; existing holders absorb it.

cards.q: A ₹1 cr SAFE with a ₹10 cr post-money cap converts in a round priced above the cap. Before the new round's own dilution, the SAFE holder owns about…
cards.explain: With a post-money cap, ownership = investment ÷ cap = 1 ÷ 10 = 10%, before new money dilutes it.

notes.p:
Startups trade **ownership for capital**. Each round brings money that should increase the company's value faster than it dilutes the founders. The **cap table** is the ledger of that trade. Understanding it protects founders from bad surprises and helps employees understand what their ESOPs are worth.

The big idea: **dilution is not loss**. Owning 56% of a ₹100 cr company is better than 100% of a ₹10 cr one. What matters is whether each round buys enough progress to raise the value per share.

points: **Pre-money / post-money**: post = pre + new money; investor % = new money ÷ post.
**Price per share** = pre-money ÷ fully diluted pre-money shares (including the pool).
**Fully diluted**: count all shares, options and convertibles as if exercised/converted.
**ESOP pool**: shares reserved for employees; vesting typically over 4 years with a 1-year cliff.
**Instruments**: equity shares (founders), **compulsorily convertible preference shares** (common for Indian VC deals), convertible notes, SAFE-like instruments.
**Down round**: a round priced below the previous round, triggering anti-dilution protections and hurting morale.

notes.h: Worked example: from founding to Series A (illustrative)
notes.p:
**Start**: two founders, 50% each.

**Seed**: raise ₹4 cr at ₹16 cr pre-money; investor requires a 10% post-money ESOP pool inside the pre-money.
Post-money = ₹20 cr. Seed investor = 4 ÷ 20 = **20%**. ESOP = **10%**. Founders = 100 − 20 − 10 = **70%** (35% each).
Founders' effective pre-money = 70% × 20 = **₹14 cr**, not ₹16 cr — the pool shuffle cost them ₹2 cr of headline valuation.

**Series A**: raise ₹20 cr at ₹80 cr pre-money (no pool top-up).
Retention factor = 80 ÷ 100 = 0.8.
Founders 70% → **56%** (28% each); ESOP 10% → **8%**; Seed 20% → **16%**; Series A **20%**. Sum = 56 + 8 + 16 + 20 = 100 ✓.

**Paper value**: founders' stake is worth 56% × ₹100 cr = ₹56 cr, up from ₹14 cr after seed. Seed investor's 16% = ₹16 cr, a 4× markup on ₹4 cr.

**Adding a SAFE**: suppose before the seed, an angel had put ₹1 cr into a post-money SAFE with a ₹10 cr cap. At conversion it would own 1 ÷ 10 = 10% (before the seed investor's dilution), which comes out of the founders' share. Many founders stack several SAFEs and are surprised by the total dilution — model every instrument in the cap table.

notes.h: The Indian startup ecosystem: what's different
notes.p: India's ecosystem grew into one of the world's largest by number of startups and unicorns, with hubs in Bengaluru, Delhi NCR and Mumbai. Some local features matter for fundraising:
points: **DPIIT recognition** under the Startup India programme unlocks certain benefits, including tax and compliance relaxations.
**Foreign investment** follows FEMA and RBI pricing and reporting rules; instruments must be permitted types (equity, CCPS, CCDs, and convertible notes for eligible startups).
**Angel tax** (Section 56(2)(viib)) long troubled startups raising above fair value; the Union Budget 2024 announced its abolition — check current law before advising.
**Flips**: many startups historically incorporated a parent abroad (often US or Singapore); several have since 'reverse-flipped' to India ahead of Indian IPOs.
Indian investors commonly negotiate detailed **shareholders' agreements** with affirmative vote rights.
Negotiating only headline valuation and ignoring the **pool shuffle**, preferences and vetoes.
Founders splitting equity 50/50 without **vesting** — if one leaves after six months, they keep half the company.
Raising too little (runs out before milestones) or too much at too high a price (sets up a down round).
Losing track of convertibles until they convert.
Giving early advisers large equity grants without vesting.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: VC and startup-finance interviews ask you to **build a cap table** across two or three rounds and compute founder ownership — practise doing it in percentages using the retention factor. Employees evaluating offers should ask: total fully diluted shares, latest preferred price, strike price, vesting, and liquidation preference stack. Founders use cap-table models to plan how much to raise and at what dilution (often roughly 10–25% per round).

points: Post-money = pre-money + investment; investor % = investment ÷ post.
Existing holders' new % = old % × pre ÷ post.
ESOP pool in the pre-money dilutes only existing holders (the pool shuffle).
Dilution is fine if value per share rises.
Convertible notes and SAFEs convert later at a cap and/or discount — model them.
Indian deals: CCPS, FEMA rules, DPIIT recognition, detailed SHAs.
Founder vesting protects everyone if a co-founder leaves.

chapters.title: Scaling: hiring, culture and when to pivot

cards.title: Scaling changes the job
cards.body: At 10 people, founders do the work. At 100, they build the team that does it. At 1,000, they design the **system** — structure, processes, culture, metrics. Many founders struggle because the skills that won the first stage aren't the ones the next stage needs.

cards.title: Hiring is the main lever
cards.body: Early hires shape culture and the bar for everyone after them. Hire for **slope** (learning speed) and ownership early; add specialists as functions mature. Write the role's outcomes before writing the job description, and use structured interviews and work samples rather than gut feel.

cards.title: Culture = what is rewarded
cards.body: Culture isn't values posters; it's **who gets hired, promoted and fired, and what behaviour is tolerated**. Netflix's widely shared culture deck (2009) described 'freedom and responsibility'. Ben Horowitz's *What You Do Is Who You Are* argues culture is set by leaders' actions, not slogans.

cards.title: Process arrives just in time
