cards.body: Too little process at 200 people causes chaos; too much at 20 kills speed. Add structure when the same problem recurs: OKRs for alignment, a hiring loop, a weekly business review, clear decision rights (e.g. RACI or a 'single-threaded owner').

cards.title: Worked: hiring maths
cards.body: A sales team needs 40 new reps this year. If 1 in 25 applicants gets an offer and 80% accept: 40 ÷ 0.8 = **50 offers**, × 25 = **1,250 applicants**. Add 20% first-year attrition and you must hire 50 to keep 40 → ~63 offers and ~1,560 applicants. Recruiting capacity is a real growth constraint.

cards.title: When to pivot
cards.body: Signals: retention stays flat-low after many iterations, CAC keeps rising, customers like it but won't pay, or the market is too small. Pivot one dimension at a time — segment, problem, channel or model. Meesho, for example, started as a local-fashion discovery app before pivoting to social commerce for resellers.

cards.title: Founder mode vs managers
cards.body: Reid Hoffman's *Blitzscaling* argues for speed over efficiency when markets are winner-take-most — but it is a deliberate, risky choice, not a default. Blitzscaling without unit economics is just burning cash faster.

cards.q: You need to hire 30 engineers; 1 in 20 candidates gets an offer and 75% accept. How many candidates should enter the funnel?
cards.explain: Offers needed = 30 ÷ 0.75 = 40; candidates = 40 × 20 = 800.

cards.q: Which best describes a company's real culture?
options: Behaviour leaders reward, tolerate and punish
cards.explain: Culture is revealed by consequences — hiring, promotion and firing decisions.

cards.q: Which is the strongest signal to consider a pivot?
options: Retention remains low across many product iterations and cohorts
cards.explain: Persistent low retention despite iteration suggests the core value hypothesis is wrong.

notes.p:
Finding product–market fit is the first miracle; **scaling** is the second. Growth breaks things: communication fails as headcount rises, quality slips, founders become bottlenecks, culture dilutes. Scaling well means building an organisation that can keep delivering the core value to ten or a hundred times more customers — while keeping speed.

The central insight: what got you here won't get you there. The founder who personally closed every deal must now hire, coach and trust a sales leader.

points: **Family (1–15 people)**: everyone talks daily; no managers; hire generalists who learn fast.
**Tribe (15–50)**: first managers and functions; informal communication starts failing.
**Village (50–150)**: needs explicit priorities (OKRs), a hiring process, onboarding, documented decisions. Robin Dunbar's research on group size is often cited around ~150.
**City (150–1,000+)**: layers, specialised functions, formal planning, compliance, a professional HR and finance team.
These thresholds are heuristics, not laws; the point is that each stage needs different systems.

notes.p:
**Principles**: hire ahead of need for critical roles (a good CFO before an IPO, not after); define outcomes ('reduce delivery time to 30 minutes in 3 cities by Q4') before titles; use **structured interviews** with the same questions and scoring rubric for all candidates — research in organisational psychology consistently finds structured interviews and work samples predict performance better than unstructured chats.

**Worked example (illustrative)**: a B2B startup plans to grow sales reps from 20 to 60 in a year. Conversion: 1 in 25 applicants gets an offer, 80% accept, and 20% of new hires leave in year one. Net new reps needed = 40. Gross hires to net 40 after 20% attrition = 40 ÷ 0.8 = 50. Offers = 50 ÷ 0.8 = 62.5 ≈ 63. Applicants = 63 × 25 ≈ **1,575**. Ramp time of 3 months per rep means revenue lags hiring — finance must fund salaries before reps produce. This is why scaling plans fail when recruiting is treated as an afterthought.

Culture is the set of behaviours that are **rewarded and tolerated**. Netflix's 2009 culture deck, shared publicly by Reed Hastings, became influential for ideas such as 'keeper test' and context over control (later expanded in *No Rules Rules*, 2020, with Erin Meyer). Indian companies have their own versions — Infosys emphasised transparency and governance in its early decades; Zerodha has spoken about frugality and avoiding aggressive sales practices.

Practical tools: write down a few **operating principles** with examples of what they mean in decisions; let leaders model them visibly; make promotions consistent with them; and fire brilliant jerks. Culture breaks fastest when a high performer is visibly excused from the rules.

notes.h: When to pivot — and when to persevere
notes.p:
Pivot signals: flat-low retention after real iteration, rising CAC with no organic pull, customers who praise but don't pay, a market that proves too small, or a structural change (regulation, a giant entering). Persevere signals: improving cohorts, rising willingness to pay, a segment that loves you even if others don't.

Well-known pivots: Slack (from a game), Instagram (from Burbn), and in India **Meesho**, which began as a hyperlocal fashion discovery app (Fashnear) before focusing on resellers selling via WhatsApp and social media, later broadening into a marketplace. Good pivots keep the team's hard-won learning and assets and change one big assumption.

points: **Premature scaling**: hiring and spending ahead of product–market fit — often cited in startup post-mortems.
Hiring for experience at big companies without checking fit for a startup's ambiguity.
Founders refusing to delegate, becoming the bottleneck for every decision.
Adding process for its own sake, or never adding it.
Ignoring first-time managers' training — most promoted individual contributors need help managing.
Pivoting from panic rather than evidence.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Founders' office, chief-of-staff and strategy roles at startups often involve exactly these problems: building hiring plans, designing OKRs, writing org charts, and running weekly business reviews. Interview prompts: 'Our startup is growing from 50 to 300 people next year — what breaks first?' (communication, hiring bar, decision rights, first-time managers). Organisational behaviour exams may ask about culture, structure and the Greiner growth model, which describes phases of growth separated by crises (leadership, autonomy, control, red tape).

points: Scaling changes the founder's job from doing to building systems and teams.
Hiring is the main lever; use structured interviews and plan funnels with conversion rates.
Culture = behaviours rewarded and tolerated; leaders set it by actions.
Add process just in time — when problems recur.
Blitzscaling is a deliberate bet, not a default.
Pivot on evidence (persistent low retention, no willingness to pay), one dimension at a time.
Premature scaling is a classic startup killer.

chapters.title: Product management for MBAs: discovery, prioritisation and roadmaps

cards.title: What a PM actually owns
cards.body: A product manager owns the **'what' and 'why'** of a product — which problems to solve, for whom, and how success is measured. Engineers own 'how'; designers own the experience. PMs lead without authority, so their tools are evidence, clarity and trust.

cards.title: Four product risks
cards.body: Marty Cagan (*Inspired*) says good product teams tackle four risks before building: **value** (will customers buy/use it?), **usability** (can they figure it out?), **feasibility** (can we build it?), and **business viability** (does it work for legal, finance, sales, brand?).

cards.title: Discovery before delivery
cards.body: **Discovery** = finding the right thing to build: customer interviews, data analysis, prototypes, usability tests. **Delivery** = building it right. Teresa Torres's **opportunity solution tree** links a desired outcome → customer opportunities (needs, pains) → candidate solutions → experiments.

cards.title: RICE prioritisation
cards.body: **RICE score = Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort.** Reach = users affected per period; Impact = scale like 3 (massive), 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25; Confidence = % certainty; Effort = person-months. Popularised by Intercom, it forces explicit assumptions instead of the loudest voice winning.

cards.title: Worked: RICE
cards.body: A: reach 5,000, impact 2, confidence 80%, effort 4 → **2,000**. B: reach 20,000, impact 0.5, confidence 100%, effort 2 → **5,000**. C: reach 2,000, impact 3, confidence 50%, effort 1 → **3,000**. Order: B, C, A — the small, broad improvement beats the flashy feature.

cards.title: Roadmaps that don't lie
cards.body: Feature-and-date roadmaps imply certainty you don't have. Many teams prefer **outcome-based** or **Now / Next / Later** roadmaps: committed work now, likely bets next, themes later. Tie each item to a metric — e.g. 'raise week-4 retention from 25% to 30%'.

cards.title: PM interview tip
cards.body: For 'Design a product for X' questions: clarify the goal → pick a user segment → list pain points → prioritise one → brainstorm solutions → choose with trade-offs → define success metrics. For 'Metric dropped 10%' questions: check data issues, segment by time, platform, geography and funnel step before guessing causes.

cards.q: Feature X: reach 8,000, impact 1, confidence 50%, effort 2. RICE score?
Testing whether customers actually want a feature addresses which of Cagan's risks?
cards.explain: Value risk asks whether customers will choose to use or buy it.

cards.q: A 'Now / Next / Later' roadmap mainly helps by…
options: Fixing exact launch dates for two years
Communicating priorities while being honest about uncertainty
cards.explain: It separates committed near-term work from less certain future bets.

notes.p:
A product manager's job is to make sure the team builds **something customers value that also works for the business**. The role sits at the intersection of customers, technology and business — which is why MBAs often move into it. PMs rarely have formal authority over engineers or designers; they lead by bringing clarity on the problem, evidence about customers and a sharp definition of success.

India has a deep PM job market across consumer internet (Flipkart, Swiggy, Zomato, PhonePe, Meesho), SaaS (Freshworks, Zoho), fintech and the India offices of global firms.

points: **Outcomes over outputs**: the goal is a change in customer behaviour or a business metric, not 'shipped 12 features'.
**Discovery**: interview users, study funnels and cohorts, map the opportunity space (Torres's opportunity solution tree), prototype and test.
**Four risks** (Cagan): value, usability, feasibility, business viability — retire them cheaply before committing engineers.
**Prioritise**: RICE, ICE (Impact, Confidence, Ease), cost of delay, or the **Kano model** (Noriaki Kano) — basic needs, performance needs and 'delighters'.
**Specify**: a short PRD — problem, users, success metrics, scope, non-goals, open questions.
**Deliver and learn**: ship in increments, run A/B tests, review metrics, iterate.

notes.h: Worked example: prioritising a food-delivery backlog (illustrative)
notes.p:
A PM at a food-delivery app has three candidates for next quarter:

**A. Group ordering** (friends add items to one cart): reach 5,000 orders/quarter, impact 2, confidence 80%, effort 4 person-months → 5,000 × 2 × 0.8 ÷ 4 = **2,000**.
**B. Faster checkout** (save address and UPI handle, one-tap reorder): reach 20,000, impact 0.5, confidence 100%, effort 2 → **5,000**.
**C. Diet filters** (high-protein, Jain, low-oil): reach 2,000, impact 3, confidence 50%, effort 1 → **3,000**.

RICE ranks **B > C > A**. But scores are inputs to judgement, not verdicts. The PM checks strategy: if the company goal this year is to win office lunches, group ordering might jump the queue. She also notes C's confidence is low — a cheap experiment (a filter on one city) could raise confidence before full investment. The written scores make this debate explicit.

A roadmap communicates **direction and priorities**, not a contract. Good practice: organise by **themes and outcomes** ('reduce cancellations', 'improve first-week retention'); use **Now / Next / Later** horizons (associated with Janna Bastow of ProdPad); and separate committed dates (needed for marketing or regulators) from aspirations.

Metrics: pick a **North Star metric** that captures delivered customer value (e.g. weekly orders per active user), with input metrics teams can move, and **guardrail metrics** to avoid harm (cancellation rate, support tickets, app crashes). Frameworks like Google's **HEART** (Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success) help structure UX metrics.

points: **Feature factory**: measuring success by shipping, not outcomes.
**HiPPO decisions** (highest paid person's opinion) instead of evidence.
**Building for the loudest customer**, especially in B2B, and creating a bespoke mess.
**False precision in RICE**: arguing over decimals when the inputs are guesses.
**Skipping discovery** because 'we already know what users want'.
**MBA-PM trap**: writing slide decks and specs instead of talking to users and working closely with engineers.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: PM interviews in India typically include **product design** ('Design a feature for elderly UPI users'), **product improvement** ('How would you improve IRCTC?'), **metrics / root cause** ('Swiggy orders fell 8% last week — why?'), **estimation**, and **strategy** ('Should Zomato launch X?'). Structure answers clearly, state assumptions, and always close with success metrics and trade-offs. On the job, expect weekly metric reviews, sprint planning, stakeholder alignment and lots of customer conversations.

Consider how a PM might run one cycle end to end. **Outcome**: raise orders per monthly user. **Discovery**: data shows 40% of orders repeat a previous basket; interviews reveal users scroll through history every time. **Opportunity**: 'I want my usual dinner in two taps.' **Solutions**: a reorder card on the home screen, a saved-basket feature, a scheduled weekly order. **Experiment**: ship the reorder card to 10% of users for two weeks; primary metric orders per user, guardrails cancellation rate and average order value. **Result**: orders per user up 3% with no guardrail harm → roll out, then test saved baskets next. Notice the PM never argued from opinion: every step had a metric and a decision rule.

points: PMs own the 'what' and 'why'; engineers own 'how'.
Cagan's four risks: value, usability, feasibility, viability.
Discovery (right thing) precedes delivery (thing right); use opportunity solution trees.
RICE = Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort; Kano separates basics, performance, delighters.
Outcome-based Now/Next/Later roadmaps beat date-feature lists.
North Star + input + guardrail metrics.
Interview structure: goal → user → pain → solutions → prioritise → metrics.

chapters.title: Platform businesses and two-sided markets

cards.title: Pipes vs platforms
cards.body: A **pipeline** business makes something and sells it (a car maker, a paint company). A **platform** creates value by **connecting groups** — buyers and sellers, riders and drivers, payers and merchants — and lets them transact. The platform often owns little inventory; its asset is the network and the rules.

cards.title: Network effects
cards.body: **Direct**: more users make it better for users (WhatsApp). **Indirect / cross-side**: more of one side attracts the other (more sellers on Flipkart → more buyers → more sellers). Strong network effects can create winner-take-most markets — but only if users don't easily use rivals too.

cards.title: Chicken-and-egg problem
cards.body: No buyers without sellers; no sellers without buyers. Tactics: **subsidise** one side (riders get discounts, drivers get incentives), **seed supply** yourself (Amazon as its own first seller), **single-player value** (a tool useful even without the network), **piggyback** on an existing network, and **start in a small niche** (one city, one campus).

cards.title: Who pays? Pricing two sides
cards.body: Platforms often subsidise the side whose participation is most valuable to the other and harder to attract — the **money side** pays more. Shoppers pay nothing to browse; sellers pay commissions. Rochet and Tirole's work on two-sided markets formalised this pricing logic.

cards.title: Case: UPI
cards.body: UPI, built by NPCI and launched in 2016, is a **public digital platform**: banks and apps (PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm) plug in; any user can pay any merchant. Interoperability plus zero merchant fees for most UPI transactions drove huge adoption — but also raised the question of who funds the system's costs.

cards.title: Threats to platforms
cards.body: **Multi-homing**: drivers run Ola and Uber at once; sellers list on Amazon and Flipkart — weakening lock-in. **Disintermediation**: a customer and a plumber found via an app swap numbers and leave. **Regulation**: rules on competition, data and marketplace conduct. Platforms respond with trust, payments, insurance and loyalty.

cards.title: Metrics that matter
cards.body: Track **liquidity** — the chance a buyer finds a match quickly (e.g. ride ETA under 5 minutes, search-to-order conversion). Also GMV vs **take rate** (platform revenue ÷ GMV), repeat rate on each side and match quality. GMV without liquidity or take rate means little.

cards.q: More riders attract more drivers, which shortens wait times and attracts more riders. This is a…
cards.explain: Value to one side increases with participation of the other side.

cards.q: Which most weakens a platform's network-effect advantage?
cards.explain: If users and suppliers can cheaply use rivals simultaneously, the network doesn't lock them in.

cards.q: A platform has GMV of ₹2,000 cr and net revenue of ₹300 cr. Its take rate is…

notes.p:
Some of the most valuable companies of the past two decades are **platforms**: Google, Apple's App Store, Amazon Marketplace, Uber, Airbnb — and in India, Flipkart, Zomato, Swiggy, Urban Company, Meesho and the public UPI rails. A platform creates value by **facilitating interactions** between distinct groups, setting rules and building trust. Its key asset is not a factory but a **network**.

The classic texts are Rochet and Tirole's academic work on two-sided markets (early 2000s) and *Platform Revolution* (2016) by Geoffrey Parker, Marshall Van Alstyne and Sangeet Paul Choudary.

notes.h: How platforms create and capture value
points: **Matching**: reduce search costs (find a ride, a seller, a plumber).
**Trust**: ratings, reviews, verified identities, escrow, returns, insurance.
**Tools**: payments, logistics, analytics for sellers, navigation for drivers.
**Capture**: commission (take rate), listing fees, advertising, subscriptions (Swiggy One, Zomato Gold-type memberships), payments or lending margins.
**Network effects**: direct (same-side) and cross-side; can be negative too — too many sellers make search worse; surge-priced congestion annoys riders.
**Start narrow**: Facebook began on one campus; Indian food-delivery startups typically launched city by city, even neighbourhood by neighbourhood, to reach density.
**Subsidise the harder side**: ride-hailing firms paid drivers guaranteed incentives in early days so riders found cars quickly.
**Be your own supply**: Amazon sold its own inventory before opening to third-party sellers; Zomato initially digitised restaurant menus itself to build listings.
**Single-player mode**: a tool valuable alone — e.g. billing software for shops that later becomes a B2B marketplace.
**Piggyback**: PayPal grew on eBay; Airbnb is widely reported to have used Craigslist listings early on.
**Government as platform builder**: UPI scaled because NPCI made it **interoperable** — any bank, any app — so network effects accrued to the whole system, not one company.

notes.p:
A home-services marketplace in one city:

**Monthly GMV** = 40,000 jobs × ₹800 average = **₹3.2 cr**.
**Take rate** 20% → platform revenue **₹64 lakh**.
Variable costs (payment fees, insurance, customer support) ₹80 per job → ₹32 lakh.
**Contribution** = ₹64 lakh − ₹32 lakh = **₹32 lakh**.
Provider incentives to retain top professionals ₹12 lakh and consumer discounts ₹10 lakh → contribution after incentives = **₹10 lakh**.

The tension: raising the take rate to 25% adds ₹16 lakh of revenue — but if it pushes professionals to take customers offline (disintermediation), jobs fall. Urban Company-style platforms counter this by adding value that is hard to replicate offline: training, standardised pricing, guarantees and insurance, and a steady flow of jobs.

points: **Confusing GMV with revenue** — a platform's revenue is GMV × take rate.
**Assuming network effects are permanent**: multi-homing and low switching costs erode them (food-delivery restaurants list on both main apps).
**Subsidising forever**: subsidies should buy liquidity that later sustains itself; if users leave when discounts stop, the network isn't real.
**Ignoring local network effects**: a ride network in Delhi does nothing for riders in Pune; each city must reach density separately.
**Neglecting governance**: fake reviews, counterfeit products and unsafe providers destroy trust fast.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Strategy and consulting cases often ask: 'Should a platform enter a new city / category?' (density, liquidity, CAC on both sides, take rate). PM interviews ask how to solve cold start or measure marketplace health. Exams test definitions: two-sided market, network effects (direct vs indirect), multi-homing, take rate, disintermediation. In real jobs at marketplaces, you'll manage supply–demand balance, incentives and city-level P&Ls.

notes.h: Platform strategy: open vs closed, and envelopment
notes.p: Platforms also choose how **open** to be. Android licensed its OS widely to win share; Apple keeps iOS closed to control quality and capture margins. Open platforms grow faster; closed ones capture more value per user. A second strategic idea is **platform envelopment** (Eisenmann, Parker and Van Alstyne, 2006): a platform with an overlapping user base bundles a neighbouring platform's function into its own — think of super-apps adding payments, shopping and bill-pay on top of a messaging or payments base. Defend against it by deepening unique value on your side of the network, not just by matching features.

points: Platforms create value by connecting groups and setting rules; pipelines make and sell.
Network effects: direct (same side) and cross-side; they can also be negative.
Solve chicken-and-egg: start narrow, subsidise the harder side, seed supply, single-player value, piggyback.
Price the sides differently; the 'money side' pays more.
Revenue = GMV × take rate; watch liquidity and repeat rates.
Threats: multi-homing, disintermediation, regulation.
UPI shows a public, interoperable platform model.

chapters.title: Growth marketing: funnels, retention cohorts and virality

cards.title: AARRR: the pirate funnel
cards.body: Dave McClure's 'Startup Metrics for Pirates' (2007): **Acquisition** (they arrive), **Activation** (first good experience), **Retention** (they come back), **Referral** (they bring others), **Revenue** (they pay). Find the weakest stage and fix that first — usually activation or retention, not acquisition.

cards.title: Activation: the 'aha' moment
cards.body: Users who reach a key early action retain far better. Classic examples: a social app found users who connected with enough friends quickly tended to stay; for a UPI app it might be the first successful payment. Find your aha moment from data, then redesign onboarding to get users there fast.

cards.title: Cohorts, not averages
cards.body: A **cohort** is a group that started in the same period. Track what % of each cohort is still active in month 1, 2, 3… Averages mix old loyal users with new ones and hide decay. Cohort tables show whether the product — and newer users — are getting better or worse.

cards.title: Worked: reading a cohort table
cards.body: Jan cohort (1,000 users, mostly organic): month-1 45%, M2 35%, M3 30%, M4 28%, M6 27% — **flattens**, a good sign. Mar cohort (3,000, mostly paid ads): M1 30%, M2 18%, M3 12%, M4 9% — **still falling**. Paid growth is bringing weaker users; fix targeting or onboarding before spending more.

cards.title: Viral coefficient
cards.body: **K = invites sent per user × conversion rate of an invite.** If each user invites 4 people and 15% join, K = 0.6. Starting from 1,000 users, total ≈ 1,000 ÷ (1 − K) = **2,500**. Only K > 1 means self-sustaining growth; most products live below 1, where virality **amplifies** other channels.

cards.title: Growth loops beat funnels
cards.body: A **loop** feeds its own output back in: users create content → content ranks on Google → new users arrive → they create content. Referral loops (Dropbox's free storage for invites), content loops (YouTube), paid loops (revenue funds ads). Loops compound; one-off campaigns don't.

cards.title: Experiment discipline
cards.body: Run A/B tests with a pre-set primary metric, sample size and duration. Beware novelty effects, peeking at results early, and winning on clicks while losing on retention. A 'growth hack' that spams users can raise K this month and destroy trust next month.

cards.q: Each user invites 5 people and 10% accept. Starting with 2,000 users, the eventual total from virality alone is about…
A retention curve that keeps declining towards zero for every cohort most likely signals…
cards.explain: Healthy products show curves that flatten at a stable level.

cards.q: In AARRR, a user completing a first successful order is part of…
cards.explain: Activation is the first moment of real value — the 'aha' experience.

notes.p:
Growth is not 'more ads'. Sustainable growth comes from a product people value, a way to reach them efficiently, and mechanisms that make each new user help bring the next. **Growth marketing** combines marketing, product and data: instrument the funnel, find the biggest leak, run experiments, and build compounding loops.

The discipline matured in Silicon Valley in the late 2000s (the term 'growth hacker' is credited to Sean Ellis, 2010) and became standard in Indian consumer internet — from Paytm's cashback campaigns to CRED's member rewards and Meesho's reseller referrals.

points: **Acquisition**: channels — SEO, content, paid social/search, app-store optimisation, influencers, partnerships, offline. Measure CAC by channel.
**Activation**: % of new users reaching the aha moment within a set time (e.g. first order within 7 days).
**Retention**: cohort curves; daily/weekly/monthly active ratios (e.g. DAU/MAU for stickiness).
**Referral**: invites per user, invite conversion, viral cycle time.
**Revenue**: conversion to paid, ARPU, LTV.
Many practitioners re-order it as 'retention first': there is no point pouring users into a leaky bucket.

notes.p:
An edtech app tracks monthly active users by signup month (percent still active):

**Jan cohort** — 1,000 users, mostly word of mouth: M1 45%, M2 35%, M3 30%, M4 28%, M5 27%, M6 27%.
**Mar cohort** — 3,000 users, mostly from a big paid campaign: M1 30%, M2 18%, M3 12%, M4 9%.

**Reading it**: the January curve **flattens** around 27% — a core of learners gets lasting value. The March cohort is larger but decays faster. By month 4, Jan has 280 active users from 1,000; March has 270 from 3,000. The company tripled acquisition and got roughly the same retained base, at much higher cost.

**Actions**: (1) diagnose: are paid users a different segment (e.g. casual browsers attracted by a discount)? (2) improve onboarding to reach the aha moment — completing the first full lesson and practice test; (3) retarget spend toward channels with better M3 retention; (4) report blended MAU growth **and** cohort retention to leadership so a headline number doesn't mislead.

**Viral coefficient K** = (invites per user) × (invite conversion). With seed users N and K < 1, the total reached through viral generations is N × (1 + K + K² + …) = N ÷ (1 − K). Example: 1,000 users, 4 invites each, 15% conversion → K = 0.6 → about 2,500 users in total. **Cycle time** matters as much: K = 0.6 with a 1-day cycle beats K = 0.6 with a 30-day cycle.

Famous examples: Hotmail added a sign-up link at the bottom of every email in the 1990s; Dropbox offered free storage to both referrer and invitee; WhatsApp grew because using it meant inviting your contacts. In India, UPI apps used cashback for both sender and receiver, building payment networks quickly — though cashback-driven users often churned once rewards fell.

**Growth loops** (a framing popularised by Reforge) treat growth as systems where outputs re-enter as inputs — user-generated content, referrals, or revenue reinvested in ads.

points: **Vanity metrics**: downloads and registered users instead of active, retained users.
**Scaling paid acquisition before fixing retention** — the leaky bucket.
**Discount addiction**: users acquired by deep cashback leave when it stops.
**Bad A/B testing**: stopping as soon as results look significant (peeking), too many simultaneous metrics, ignoring long-term effects.
**Spammy referrals** that annoy users' contacts and damage the brand.
**Ignoring channel saturation**: CAC rises as you exhaust the most interested audience.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Marketing, PM and growth interviews ask: 'DAU fell 10% — diagnose it', 'How would you grow a new UPI app in tier-3 towns?', 'Read this cohort table'. Strong answers segment the funnel, name the weakest stage with evidence, and propose experiments with metrics. On the job, growth teams own dashboards (funnel, cohorts, CAC by channel), an experiment backlog and weekly reviews with product and marketing.

points: AARRR: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue (McClure, 2007).
Fix the leakiest stage first — usually activation or retention.
Analyse cohorts; healthy retention curves flatten.
K = invites per user × conversion; total ≈ N ÷ (1 − K) when K < 1.
Viral cycle time matters as much as K.
Growth loops compound; campaigns don't.
Avoid vanity metrics, discount addiction and peeking in A/B tests.

chapters.title: Pricing strategy deep dive: value, freemium, tiers and dynamic pricing

cards.title: Price is the most powerful lever
cards.body: A 1% price rise, with volume unchanged, flows straight to profit. For a firm with an 8% operating margin, +1% price lifts profit by about 12.5%. Yet many companies set prices by habit — cost-plus or copying competitors — instead of by **value to the customer**.

cards.title: Three anchors for price
cards.body: **Cost** sets the floor. **Customer value** sets the ceiling. **Competition** shows where you sit in between. Value-based pricing asks: what is our product worth versus the next-best alternative? That difference — **economic value to the customer (EVC)** — is the room you have to price.

cards.title: Price-change breakeven
cards.body: For a price **cut** of x% with contribution margin m, volume must rise by **x ÷ (m − x)** to keep profit unchanged. At 40% margin, a 10% cut needs 10 ÷ 30 = **+33% volume**. For a price **rise**, volume can fall by **x ÷ (m + x)**: 10 ÷ 50 = **20%** before profit drops.

cards.title: Freemium
cards.body: Give a useful free tier; charge for more features, capacity or teams. Works when free users are cheap to serve and create value (virality, network, content) and when upgrade triggers are natural. Conversion to paid is often low single-digit percentages, so the funnel must be large.

cards.title: Tiering and the decoy
cards.body: **Good–better–best** tiers let customers self-select by willingness to pay. A middle tier often wins most sales. Dan Ariely's *Predictably Irrational* described a magazine offer where a print-only option at the same price as print + web made the bundle look like a bargain — the **decoy effect**.

cards.title: Dynamic pricing
cards.body: Prices that change with demand, time or capacity: airline fares, hotel rates, ride-hailing surge, Indian Railways' flexi-fare on premium trains. It improves utilisation and revenue, but feels unfair when it spikes in emergencies. Caps, transparency and consistency protect trust.

cards.title: Price the metric customers value
cards.body: Choose a **value metric** that grows as the customer gets more value: per seat, per transaction, per GB, per order. Zoho, Freshworks and most SaaS firms price per user per month by tier; payment gateways price per transaction. A misaligned metric creates churn or leaves money on the table.

cards.q: Contribution margin 50%. To justify a 10% price cut, volume must rise by at least…
Contribution margin 30%. After a 5% price increase, how much volume can you lose before profit falls?
Value-based pricing sets the price primarily by reference to…
options: What the product is worth to the customer versus alternatives
cards.explain: Value to the customer (EVC) sets the ceiling and guides the price.

notes.p:
Of the four Ps, **price** is the only one that brings in money; the rest cost money. Analyses of large companies — such as the McKinsey study by Marn and Rosiello (HBR, 1992) — showed that a 1% improvement in price, with volume held steady, raises operating profit far more than a 1% improvement in volume or cost. The logic is simple: if your margin is 8%, an extra 1% of price is 1/8 = 12.5% more profit.

Great pricing starts with **value**: understand what customers are trying to achieve, what alternatives they have, and how much better you are. Then design price levels, structures and metrics that capture a fair share of that value.

points: **Cost-plus**: price = cost × (1 + markup). Simple, ignores customers. Fine for commodities or government contracts.
**Competition-based**: price relative to rivals; useful in transparent markets.
**Value-based**: EVC = reference value (price of next-best alternative) + differentiation value (extra benefits − extra costs). Price somewhere between cost and EVC.
**Structures**: freemium, tiered (good–better–best), usage-based, subscription, bundling, two-part tariffs (fee + usage), dynamic/surge.
**Price discrimination**: different prices for different segments — student discounts, regional pricing, time-based fares, coupons.
**Psychology**: anchoring, decoy, charm prices (₹99, ₹499), framing ('₹10 a day' vs '₹3,650 a year').

notes.h: Worked example 1: should a café chain cut prices? (illustrative)
notes.p:
A café sells 1,000 coffees a day at ₹200; variable cost ₹120 → contribution ₹80 per cup (40% margin), daily contribution ₹80,000.

**Proposal**: cut price 10% to ₹180. New contribution per cup = ₹60. To keep ₹80,000, volume must be 80,000 ÷ 60 = 1,333 cups — **+33%**. Formula check: 10 ÷ (40 − 10) = 33.3% ✓.

**Alternative**: raise price 10% to ₹220 → contribution ₹100 per cup. Volume can fall to 800 cups (**−20%**) before contribution drops: 10 ÷ (40 + 10) = 20% ✓.

Unless the café expects demand to be very price-sensitive, the price rise is the safer bet — and loyal customers who value the brand may barely notice. This asymmetry is why discount wars so often destroy industry profits.

A note-taking SaaS has 1,00,000 monthly active free users. Serving each costs ₹5 a month → ₹5 lakh. 3% convert to a ₹300/month Pro plan → 3,000 payers × ₹300 = **₹9 lakh** revenue. Pro users cost ₹30 each to serve → ₹90,000. Monthly contribution = 9,00,000 − 5,00,000 − 90,000 = **₹3.1 lakh**.

Levers: raise conversion to 4% (+₹3 lakh revenue), cut free-user cost (cheaper storage), or limit the free tier so heavy users hit an upgrade trigger. Free users also bring referrals — if they lower CAC for paid users, part of their cost is really marketing.

notes.h: Tiering, bundling and dynamic pricing in practice
notes.p:
**Tiers**: streaming services in India offer mobile-only, basic and premium plans; SaaS firms such as Zoho and Freshworks use free, standard and enterprise tiers. The middle tier is often designed to be the default choice; the top tier anchors value.

**Bundling**: Jio's data-plus-apps packs and telecom family plans increase perceived value and reduce churn.

**Dynamic pricing**: airlines use revenue management (fare buckets that close as seats sell); hotels price by occupancy; ride-hailing uses surge pricing to balance drivers and riders. Indian Railways introduced a flexi-fare system on Rajdhani, Shatabdi and Duronto trains in 2016, where fares rise as seats fill. Public backlash against surge pricing during emergencies shows the trust limits — many firms cap surges or suspend them during disasters.

points: **Cost-plus by default**: leaves money on the table when value is high, overprices when value is low.
**Discounting to hit monthly targets**: trains customers to wait for deals.
**Too many tiers** causing choice overload; or tiers with no clear upgrade trigger.
**Ignoring the value metric** — e.g. flat pricing for customers whose usage varies 100×.
**Unfair-feeling dynamic pricing** that damages brand trust.
**Not testing**: price is rarely A/B tested in public, but can be tested by geography, new customers or packaging.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Consulting cases ('Our client wants to cut prices to gain share — should it?'), PM and marketing interviews ('How would you price a new subscription for a food app?'), and exams on price elasticity and the breakeven formula. In jobs, pricing managers run price-volume analyses, discount governance, and willingness-to-pay research using methods like **Van Westendorp's price-sensitivity meter** and **conjoint analysis**.

points: Small price changes have large profit effects; +1% price at 8% margin ≈ +12.5% profit.
Cost = floor, value = ceiling, competition = positioning.
Price cut breakeven volume rise = x ÷ (m − x); price rise allowable loss = x ÷ (m + x).
Freemium works when free users are cheap and create value; conversion is often low single digits.
Good–better–best tiers and decoys steer choices.
Dynamic pricing raises utilisation but must protect fairness.
Choose a value metric that scales with customer value.

chapters.title: AI and data for managers: value, build vs buy, and risks

cards.title: AI makes prediction cheap
cards.body: Agrawal, Gans and Goldfarb (*Prediction Machines*, 2018): AI's core economic effect is to make **prediction** cheap — filling in missing information. When prediction gets cheap, the value of **judgement**, **data** and **action** rises. Ask: where in our business would a better, cheaper prediction change a decision?

cards.title: Where AI creates value
cards.body: **Classic ML**: credit scoring, fraud detection, demand forecasting, recommendations, pricing. **Generative AI**: drafting text and code, summarising documents, customer support, search over company knowledge. Best targets: high-volume, repetitive decisions with measurable outcomes and good data.

cards.title: Worked: support automation ROI
cards.body: 10 lakh tickets a year at ₹100 each = ₹10 cr. An AI assistant resolves 30% (3 lakh) at ₹10 each instead of ₹100 → saving 3 lakh × ₹90 = **₹2.7 cr**. Platform, integration and a review team cost ₹80 lakh → **net ₹1.9 cr a year**, before quality effects on customer satisfaction.

cards.title: Build, buy or partner
cards.body: **Buy** (SaaS or APIs) when the use case is common and speed matters. **Build** when it uses proprietary data and is core to your advantage. **Partner/fine-tune** in between: use foundation models via API with your own data and workflows. Total cost includes data work, integration, monitoring and change management.

cards.title: Data is the real moat
cards.body: Models are increasingly available to everyone; differentiation comes from **proprietary data, workflow integration and feedback loops** (usage generates data that improves the product). Data must be clean, labelled, accessible and legally usable — often 60–80% of the effort in real projects is data work.

cards.title: Risks managers must own
cards.body: **Hallucination** (confident wrong answers), **bias** (e.g. lending models disadvantaging groups), **privacy** (India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023), **security** (prompt injection, data leaks), **IP** questions, and **over-automation** without a human for high-stakes calls. Assign an owner, test, monitor and keep humans in the loop where errors are costly.

cards.title: Start with the decision, not the model
cards.body: Good AI projects begin with a business decision and a metric (cut fraud losses 20%, halve handling time), run a small pilot with a baseline, and scale only if the gain survives real-world use. 'We need an AI strategy' without a decision to improve is a slide, not a strategy.

cards.q: According to *Prediction Machines*, as AI makes prediction cheaper, which becomes MORE valuable?
cards.explain: Complements of prediction — judgement, data and the ability to act — rise in value.

cards.q: A firm wants AI for a common task (meeting transcription) with no proprietary data advantage. The sensible default is to…
options: Build its own model from scratch
cards.explain: Buy when the use case is commoditised and speed matters; build where proprietary data creates advantage.

cards.q: An AI tool confidently cites a regulation that doesn't exist. This risk is called…
cards.explain: Generative models can produce fluent but false content — hallucination; mitigate with grounding, citations and review.

notes.p:
Managers don't need to train neural networks; they need to know **where AI changes economics** and how to deploy it responsibly. The best single lens comes from Ajay Agrawal, Joshua Gans and Avi Goldfarb's *Prediction Machines* (2018): machine learning lowers the cost of **prediction**. Fraud detection predicts whether a transaction is fraudulent; demand forecasting predicts next week's sales; a language model predicts the next words. Cheaper prediction makes its complements — **judgement** (what outcome do we prefer?), **data**, and **action** — more valuable.

Generative AI (large language models since ChatGPT's 2022 launch) widened the scope from numbers to language, code and images, making knowledge work a target.

notes.h: A map of where AI creates value
points: **Revenue**: recommendations (Netflix, Amazon), personalised offers, dynamic pricing, lead scoring.
**Cost**: support automation, document processing (KYC, invoices, claims), coding assistants, forecasting to cut inventory.
**Risk**: fraud detection in UPI and cards, credit underwriting using alternative data, anomaly detection in operations.
**New products**: AI tutors, copilots inside software, vernacular voice interfaces for Bharat users.
**Selection test**: high volume × measurable outcome × available data × tolerable error cost.

notes.h: Worked example: a customer-support AI business case (illustrative)
notes.p:
A consumer-finance company handles **10 lakh support tickets a year** at a fully loaded cost of **₹100 per ticket** = ₹10 cr.

**Pilot**: an AI assistant grounded in the company's policy documents answers routine queries (EMI dates, statement requests) in English, Hindi and Tamil, handing complex cases to humans.

**Results after scale-up**: 30% of tickets (3 lakh) resolved end-to-end at ~₹10 each → savings = 3 lakh × (100 − 10) = **₹2.7 cr**.
**Costs**: licences and API usage, integration, a quality-review team and monitoring ≈ **₹80 lakh** a year.
**Net benefit ≈ ₹1.9 cr a year.**

**What the manager must also check**: customer satisfaction on AI-handled tickets vs human; error rate on sensitive topics (wrong loan information can create regulatory issues); escalation speed; data privacy compliance. If AI-handled CSAT falls sharply, savings may be offset by churn. Decision rule set in advance: scale only if CSAT stays within 3 points of the human baseline.

**Buy** off-the-shelf tools for generic tasks (transcription, writing assistants, standard chatbots): fast, cheap, low differentiation.
**Partner / customise**: use foundation models through APIs plus your own data — retrieval over internal documents, fine-tuning, workflow integration. This is the common enterprise path.
**Build**: own models where proprietary data and scale create advantage — e.g. a large lender's credit models, a marketplace's ranking algorithms.

Total cost of ownership includes data pipelines, evaluation, monitoring for drift, security, retraining and — most underestimated — **change management**: redesigning processes and roles so people actually use the tool. Many pilots fail not on accuracy but on adoption.

points: **Hallucination**: ground answers in trusted sources, show citations, restrict scope, keep humans reviewing high-stakes outputs.
**Bias and fairness**: test outcomes across groups; Amazon reportedly scrapped an experimental recruiting tool after finding it disadvantaged women.
**Privacy**: India's **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023** sets consent and purpose-limitation duties; sector regulators (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI) add their own expectations.
**Security**: prompt injection, leakage of confidential data into external tools.
**Accountability**: name a business owner for each model, document intended use, monitor performance after launch.
**Over-trust and deskilling**: people stop checking outputs; design workflows that keep judgement active.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Consulting and strategy interviews now ask: 'How should a bank use generative AI?' or 'Build a business case for AI in a call centre.' Use the structure: decision/use case → value (with numbers) → feasibility (data, tech) → risks → pilot plan with metrics. PMs are asked how to evaluate AI features (accuracy, latency, cost per query, user trust). In jobs, managers sponsor pilots, set success metrics and govern risk with legal and compliance.

points: AI makes prediction cheap; judgement, data and action become more valuable.
Target high-volume decisions with measurable outcomes and good data.
Build a business case: baseline, savings or revenue, full costs, quality guardrails.
Buy for commodity tasks, build where proprietary data is an edge, partner in between.
Data and workflow integration are the moat; models are increasingly commoditised.
Own the risks: hallucination, bias, privacy (DPDP Act 2023), security.
Start with the decision and a pilot; scale only on measured results.

chapters.title: Building brands: brand equity, positioning and Indian cases

cards.title: What a brand really is
cards.body: A brand is the **set of associations in customers' minds** that makes them choose, trust and pay more for one product over a near-identical one. Logos and ads are tools; the brand itself lives in memory. Strong brands earn price premiums, loyalty and easier launches of new products.

cards.title: Brand equity
cards.body: **Brand equity** = the extra value a brand name adds versus an unbranded equivalent. David Aaker (*Managing Brand Equity*, 1991) listed components: **awareness, perceived quality, associations, loyalty** and other proprietary assets. Kevin Lane Keller defined **customer-based brand equity** as how knowledge of the brand changes customers' response to its marketing.

cards.title: Keller's CBBE pyramid
cards.body: Four steps, bottom to top: **Salience** (who are you?) → **Performance & Imagery** (what are you?) → **Judgements & Feelings** (what do I think and feel about you?) → **Resonance** (what about you and me? — loyalty, attachment, community, active engagement). You can't skip levels.

cards.title: A positioning statement
cards.body: **For** [target customer] **who** [need], [brand] **is** [frame of reference/category] **that** [key benefit]. **Unlike** [main alternative], **we** [point of difference, with a reason to believe]. It is an internal tool for consistency, not an ad slogan.

cards.title: Case: Cadbury Dairy Milk
cards.body: Chocolate in India was long seen largely as a children's treat. Cadbury's campaigns — from the 1990s 'Real taste of life' cricket-field dance ad to 'Kuch meetha ho jaaye' — repositioned it as part of **adult celebrations and Indian rituals** where mithai traditionally sat. A change in **frame of reference** grew the whole category.

cards.title: Case: Amul and Asian Paints
cards.body: **Amul**: the 'Amul girl' topical hoardings since the 1960s keep salience high at low cost; 'The Taste of India' links the brand to national identity and cooperative trust. **Asian Paints**: 'Har ghar kuch kehta hai' moved paint from a commodity to **self-expression and home pride**, supported by a strong dealer network.

cards.title: Consistency beats novelty
cards.body: Brands are built through **consistent** associations over years — the same distinctive assets (colours, characters, jingles, taglines). Frequent repositioning confuses memory. Byron Sharp's *How Brands Grow* argues growth comes mostly from **mental and physical availability** among many light buyers, not just loyalty.

cards.q: Which level sits at the top of Keller's CBBE pyramid?
cards.explain: Resonance — deep loyalty and engagement — is the top of the pyramid.

cards.q: In a positioning statement, 'frame of reference' means…
options: The category or competitive set the brand is compared with
cards.explain: It tells customers what the brand should be compared against, e.g. 'chocolate as celebration sweet'.

cards.q: Aaker's brand equity components include all EXCEPT…
cards.explain: Factory capacity is an operational asset, not a component of brand equity.

notes.p:
Two bottles of packaged water can be chemically identical, yet one sells at a premium. The difference is the **brand**: a bundle of memories, beliefs and feelings that reduces risk and adds meaning. Brands matter because customers can't evaluate everything; they use brands as **shortcuts** to trust, quality and identity.

For the company, a strong brand delivers pricing power, loyalty, bargaining power with retailers, lower marketing cost per sale over time, and the ability to stretch into new categories (Tata into many sectors; Amul from butter to ice cream).

notes.h: Brand equity: the two classic models
notes.p:
**Aaker (1991)**: brand equity is a set of assets and liabilities linked to a brand — **brand awareness**, **perceived quality**, **brand associations**, **brand loyalty** and other proprietary assets (patents, trademarks, channel relationships).

**Keller's Customer-Based Brand Equity (CBBE)**: brand equity is the differential effect that brand knowledge has on consumer response to marketing. Keller's pyramid builds it in four steps:
points: **Salience** — breadth and depth of awareness: is the brand recalled in the right situations?
**Performance** (functional: reliability, price, design) and **Imagery** (user profile, personality, values, history).
**Judgements** (quality, credibility, consideration, superiority) and **Feelings** (warmth, fun, security, social approval, self-respect).
**Resonance** — behavioural loyalty, attitudinal attachment, sense of community, active engagement.
Left side = rational route; right side = emotional route. Strong brands build both.

notes.h: Positioning: owning a place in the mind
notes.p: Al Ries and Jack Trout popularised **positioning** (*Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind*, 1981): a brand must own a clear, distinct place in the customer's mind relative to competitors. Practical tools:
points: **Points of parity**: what you must match to be considered (a phone must have a good camera).
**Points of difference**: what you do better, that customers value and you can prove.
**Reason to believe**: evidence for the claim (technology, heritage, testimonials).
**Positioning statement** (format popularised by Geoffrey Moore): For [target] who [need], [brand] is a [category] that [benefit]. Unlike [alternative], we [difference].
**Brand architecture**: branded house (Tata, Apple — one master brand) vs house of brands (HUL, P&G — separate brands like Surf Excel and Lifebuoy).

notes.p:
**Cadbury Dairy Milk (Mondelez)**: repositioned chocolate from kids' treat to adult celebration and festive gifting — 'Kuch meetha ho jaaye', Diwali gift packs — competing with mithai rather than just other chocolates. Changing the frame of reference expanded the market.

**Amul**: a farmer-owned cooperative brand (GCMMF) with very low advertising spend relative to its scale, relying on the long-running Amul girl topical campaign for salience and on 'The Taste of India' for meaning.

**Asian Paints**: built emotional imagery ('Har ghar kuch kehta hai') on top of performance and a deep dealer and tinting-machine network — brand plus distribution.

**Apple**: premium imagery (design, simplicity, creativity) consistently reinforced for decades; resonance shows up as community and repeat purchase.

**Fevicol (Pidilite)**: humorous ads dramatise one functional benefit — an unbreakable bond — making an industrial adhesive a household name.

notes.h: Worked example: writing a positioning statement (illustrative)
notes.p:
A new millet-based breakfast cereal brand, 'Nutri-Ragi':

**For** health-conscious urban parents **who** want a quick breakfast their children will actually eat, **Nutri-Ragi is** a ready-to-eat cereal **that** delivers the nutrition of traditional millets in a taste kids like. **Unlike** imported cornflakes, **we** use Indian millets with no added refined sugar — **reason to believe**: a recipe developed with nutritionists and an ingredient list of five items.

**CBBE plan**: salience via school-tiffin occasions and quick-commerce visibility; performance via taste tests; imagery around 'smart Indian parents'; feelings of reassurance; resonance through a parents' recipe community.

points: **Confusing brand with logo or advertising**.
**Positioning on something customers don't value** or that every competitor can claim ('best quality').
**Inconsistency**: new agency, new idea every year.
**Over-stretching**: extensions that contradict core associations.
**Short-termism**: heavy price promotions train customers to buy on deal and erode equity.
**Ignoring availability**: a loved brand that isn't on the shelf or app loses the sale.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Marketing interviews (FMCG, consumer tech) ask: 'Reposition brand X for Gen Z', 'Why is Amul so strong?', 'Write a positioning statement'. Exams test Keller's pyramid and Aaker's components. Brand managers in FMCG own a brand's P&L, run consumer research, brief agencies, plan launches and track brand-health metrics (awareness, consideration, preference, NPS).

points: A brand is the set of associations in customers' minds; equity = value added versus unbranded.
Aaker: awareness, perceived quality, associations, loyalty, other assets.
Keller CBBE: salience → performance & imagery → judgements & feelings → resonance.
Positioning: target, need, frame of reference, benefit, point of difference, reason to believe.
Branded house (Tata) vs house of brands (HUL).
Cases: Cadbury reframed its category; Amul builds salience cheaply; Asian Paints pairs emotion with distribution.
Consistency and availability drive brand growth.

chapters.title: B2B sales and key account management

cards.title: B2B buying is a group decision
cards.body: Business purchases involve a **buying centre** (Webster and Wind): **users**, **influencers**, **buyers** (procurement), **deciders**, **gatekeepers** and often finance and legal. Each wants something different. A sale is won by understanding all of them, not just the friendly contact.

cards.title: Qualifying deals
cards.body: Don't chase every lead. **BANT** checks Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline. **MEDDIC** goes deeper: Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Champion. A deal with no access to the economic buyer and no champion is a hope, not a forecast.

cards.title: SPIN and Challenger
cards.body: Neil Rackham's research (*SPIN Selling*, 1988) found successful large-deal sellers asked **Situation, Problem, Implication, Need-payoff** questions. *The Challenger Sale* (Dixon and Adamson, 2011) argued top performers **teach** customers something new, **tailor** it, and **take control** of the conversation.

cards.title: Pipeline maths
cards.body: **Pipeline needed = target ÷ win rate.** Target ₹10 cr, win rate 25% → ₹40 cr of qualified pipeline. If deals take 6 months to close, that pipeline must exist 6 months ahead. **Sales velocity** = (opportunities × win rate × average deal size) ÷ cycle length.

cards.title: Key account management
cards.body: The top 10–20% of customers often generate a large share of revenue and profit. **KAM** treats each as a mini-market: an account plan, relationship map across levels, joint business goals, quarterly business reviews, and a team (sales, delivery, finance) aligned around the client's success.

cards.title: Case: Indian IT services
cards.body: Firms like TCS, Infosys and Wipro grow largely by **mining** existing clients: starting with one project, building trust, then expanding across functions and geographies. Their annual reports track the number of clients above revenue thresholds (e.g. $1M, $10M, $100M) — a KAM metric in disguise.

cards.title: Sell outcomes, not features
cards.body: Procurement compares feature lists and prices; executives buy **outcomes** — lower downtime, faster collections, fewer errors. Quantify value in the customer's terms ('saves ₹2 cr a year in overtime') and price against it.

cards.q: Annual target ₹12 cr; historical win rate 30%. Minimum qualified pipeline needed?
In MEDDIC, the 'E' stands for…
cards.explain: The economic buyer is the person who can release the budget and approve the purchase.

cards.q: In SPIN selling, 'What happens to your month-end close when invoices are entered late?' is a…
cards.explain: Implication questions explore the consequences of a problem, raising its perceived cost.

notes.p:
B2B (business-to-business) selling is not consumer marketing with bigger cheques. Purchases are **larger, rarer, riskier and collective**: a hospital buying an imaging system, a bank buying core banking software, an automaker choosing a component supplier. Decisions take months, involve many people, and the cost of a wrong choice falls on careers. So B2B sales is about **reducing risk and proving value** for a group of stakeholders.

After the first sale, the work shifts to **key account management**: keeping, growing and deepening relationships with the customers that matter most. In many B2B firms, a large share of revenue comes from a minority of accounts — so losing one hurts badly.

points: **Prospecting**: identify target accounts (ideal customer profile), triggers (new funding, expansion, regulation).
**Qualification**: BANT or MEDDIC — is there pain, budget, an economic buyer, a decision process we understand, a champion?
**Discovery**: SPIN questions — Situation (facts), Problem (difficulties), Implication (consequences), Need-payoff (value of solving).
**Solution and proposal**: tailor to the decision criteria; build a quantified business case.
**Negotiation and procurement**: pricing, terms, legal, security reviews.
**Close and handover**: onboarding, success plan.
**Expand**: upsell, cross-sell, renewals — the KAM phase.

notes.p:
A SaaS company sells inventory software to mid-sized manufacturers.

**Target** new revenue next year: **₹12 cr**. Average deal size ₹30 lakh → **40 wins** needed. Win rate from qualified opportunity to close: **25%** → **160 qualified opportunities** (₹48 cr of pipeline). Lead-to-qualified-opportunity conversion 20% → **800 leads**. Each rep can work ~40 opportunities a year → **4 reps**, plus pre-sales support.

**Velocity check**: if each rep runs 10 open opportunities at a time with a 25% win rate, ₹30 lakh deal size and a 4-month cycle, velocity = (10 × 0.25 × 30 lakh) ÷ 4 months = **₹18.75 lakh per rep per month**, or ₹2.25 cr a year per rep. Four reps → ₹9 cr — short of target. Options: hire a fifth rep, raise win rate through better qualification, shorten the cycle with a pilot offer, or increase deal size by bundling modules. Sales planning is arithmetic first, motivation second.

**Account segmentation**: rank accounts by current value and potential (a simple 2×2: high value/high potential = strategic; high value/low potential = maintain; low value/high potential = develop; low/low = serve efficiently).

**Account plan** for each strategic account: customer's goals and pain points, relationship map (who supports us, who is neutral, who opposes), white space (products not yet sold), risks, and a 12-month action plan.

**Governance**: quarterly business reviews with value delivered in numbers; executive sponsors on both sides; joint roadmaps.

**Cases**: Indian IT services firms disclose client counts by revenue band and grow by expanding within accounts. Industrial firms such as Siemens, ABB or Thermax manage large customers through dedicated account teams. FMCG companies run KAM with modern trade and quick-commerce platforms — negotiating shelf space, promotions and joint business plans.

points: **Single-threaded relationships**: one champion leaves and the deal dies. Map and engage multiple stakeholders.
**Happy ears**: forecasting deals because the contact is friendly, without an economic buyer.
**Feature dumping** instead of diagnosing pain.
**Discounting early** instead of building value; procurement will ask for more anyway.
**Neglecting existing accounts** while chasing new logos — retention is cheaper than acquisition.
**Over-customising** for one big client, creating unprofitable complexity.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Sales and marketing roles (B2B SaaS, industrial goods, IT services, banking corporate relationship management) test whether you can run discovery and build a business case. Interview prompts: 'Sell me this software to a CFO', 'How would you grow a ₹5 cr account to ₹20 cr?', 'Your forecast missed — why?' Exams cover the buying centre, personal selling process, SPIN, and KAM. Consultants use the same frameworks when advising on sales-force effectiveness.

points: B2B buying is a group decision: users, influencers, buyers, deciders, gatekeepers.
Qualify with BANT or MEDDIC; no economic buyer or champion → weak deal.
SPIN: Situation, Problem, Implication, Need-payoff (Rackham).
Challenger: teach, tailor, take control (Dixon and Adamson).
Pipeline needed = target ÷ win rate; velocity = opps × win rate × deal size ÷ cycle.
KAM: segment accounts, plan, map relationships, review value quarterly.
Sell outcomes in the customer's numbers.

chapters.title: Hypothesis-driven problem solving, MECE and issue trees

cards.title: Start with the answer
cards.body: Consultants work **hypothesis-first**: form an early best guess ('profits fell because delivery commissions rose'), then gather only the data needed to prove or kill it. It feels backwards, but it's faster than 'boiling the ocean' — collecting everything and hoping the answer appears.

cards.title: MECE
cards.body: **Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive**: break a problem into parts that **don't overlap** and **together cover everything**. Profit = revenue − cost is MECE. 'Customers: young, urban, students' is not — groups overlap and rural older people are missing.

cards.title: Issue trees
cards.body: An **issue tree** breaks a key question into sub-questions, level by level, each MECE. **Diagnostic trees** ask 'why?' (why did profit fall?). **Solution trees** ask 'how?' (how can we grow revenue 20%?). The leaves become analyses you can assign and complete.

cards.title: Worked: a profit issue tree
cards.body: 'Why did our cinema chain's profit fall?' → Revenue (tickets = footfall × average ticket price; F&B = footfall × spend per head; advertising) vs Costs (fixed: rent, staff; variable: film distributor share, F&B cost). Data shows footfall −15% while ticket price +8% → hypothesis: OTT and high prices cut visits.

cards.title: The pyramid principle
cards.body: Barbara Minto (*The Pyramid Principle*, formerly McKinsey) says communicate **top-down**: lead with the answer, support it with 3 or so MECE arguments, each backed by data. Executives read the first line; make it the recommendation, not the background.

cards.title: 80/20 and 'so what?'
cards.body: Focus on the few drivers that explain most of the problem (Pareto). After every chart, ask **'So what?'** — what does this mean for the decision? A slide without an implication is decoration. Good consultants write the slide title as the conclusion ('Footfall decline explains 70% of profit gap').

cards.title: Kill your hypothesis fast
cards.body: The goal is truth, not being right. Design each analysis so it could **disprove** your hypothesis. If the data says no, pivot quickly and say so. Confirmation bias — only seeking supporting data — is the classic failure of hypothesis-driven work.

cards.q: Which split of 'all customers' is MECE?
options: Customers who bought in the last 12 months vs those who didn't
cards.explain: Bought vs didn't buy in a defined period covers everyone with no overlap.

cards.q: In the pyramid principle, a recommendation memo should open with…
options: A list of all data collected
cards.explain: Top-down communication: lead with the governing thought, then support it.

cards.q: A diagnostic issue tree is mainly organised around…
cards.explain: Diagnostic trees find root causes; solution trees generate options.

notes.p:
Management consulting sells **structured thinking** applied to messy problems. Three habits make it work: **start with a hypothesis**, **break problems into MECE pieces**, and **communicate top-down**. These habits are useful far beyond consulting — for a product manager diagnosing a metric drop, a CFO explaining a miss to the board, or a student answering a case interview.

The ideas are associated especially with McKinsey (described in Ethan Rasiel's *The McKinsey Way*, 1999) and Barbara Minto's *The Pyramid Principle*, but every top firm — BCG, Bain and others — trains its people in similar methods.
**Process**:
points: **Define the problem precisely**: SMART — specific, measurable, action-oriented, relevant, time-bound. 'Restore operating margin from 6% to 10% within 18 months' beats 'improve profitability'.
**Form an initial hypothesis** from experience, quick interviews and basic data (day 1).
**Build an issue tree** under the hypothesis: what must be true for it to hold?
**Plan analyses** that test each branch — the minimum data needed.
**Gather, analyse, iterate**: refine or abandon the hypothesis as evidence comes in.
**Synthesise** into a recommendation with a clear 'so what'.

notes.h: MECE and issue trees in detail
notes.p: **MECE** is a discipline for completeness without double counting. Reliable MECE splits come from:
points: **Maths identities**: profit = revenue − cost; revenue = volume × price; volume = market size × share.
**Process steps**: a customer journey (awareness → consideration → purchase → use → repeat).
**Opposites**: internal vs external; new vs existing customers; domestic vs export.
**Value chain**: sourcing → manufacturing → distribution → sales → service.
**Frameworks** (when they fit): 3Cs (company, customers, competitors), 4Ps, Porter's five forces.
A 'catch-all' bucket ('other') can make a list exhaustive — but if it is large, your structure is weak.

notes.p:
**Problem**: a multiplex chain's operating profit fell from ₹200 cr to ₹120 cr in two years.

**Level 1**: Revenue vs costs. Revenue fell ₹60 cr; costs rose ₹20 cr. Revenue explains 75% of the ₹80 cr drop — focus there first (80/20).

**Level 2 — revenue**: tickets, food & beverage, advertising.
Tickets: footfall fell from 10 crore to 8.5 crore (−15%); average ticket price rose from ₹220 to ₹238 (+8%). Ticket revenue: ₹2,200 cr → ₹2,023 cr (**−₹177 cr**).
F&B: spend per head rose from ₹120 to ₹140; revenue ₹1,200 cr → ₹1,190 cr (−₹10 cr).
Advertising: up ₹127 cr thanks to new ad formats.
Net revenue change: −177 − 10 + 127 = **−₹60 cr** ✓.

**Level 3 — footfall**: by film type and city tier. Hypothesis: mid-budget films moved to OTT; high ticket + F&B prices deter families. Analyses: footfall by film category, price elasticity by city, survey of lapsed customers.

**Synthesis (top-down)**: 'Profit fell mainly because footfall dropped 15%, driven by fewer mid-budget releases and price-sensitive families. We recommend value-day pricing and family combos in tier-2 cities, worth an estimated ₹X cr.'

points: **Boiling the ocean**: collecting all data before forming any view.
**Non-MECE buckets** that overlap ('marketing issues' and 'pricing issues' both containing discounts).
**Framework forcing**: dumping 4Ps or Porter on a problem it doesn't fit.
**Confirmation bias**: falling in love with the hypothesis.
**Bottom-up storytelling**: walking executives through 20 charts before the answer.
**No 'so what'**: interesting facts with no implication for the decision.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Every consulting case interview tests structuring: the interviewer gives a vague problem and watches how you build a MECE tree, state a hypothesis and prioritise. Strategy, product and general-management roles use the same skills in board decks, business reviews and root-cause analyses. Tip: say your structure aloud ('I'd look at this in two parts: revenue and costs…'), number your buckets, and update the hypothesis explicitly when new data arrives.

Solution trees ask 'how?' rather than 'why?'. Suppose the question is: **how can a regional bank grow fee income by ₹100 cr in three years?** Level 1 (MECE by customer type): retail, MSME, corporate. Under retail: more customers × more products per customer × higher fee per product — e.g. cross-sell insurance and mutual funds to existing account holders. Under MSME: transaction banking (cash management, trade finance), merchant acquiring. Under corporate: forex and treasury services. Each leaf gets a rough size (retail cross-sell ₹40 cr, MSME ₹35 cr, corporate ₹25 cr) so leadership can see the plan adds up — and which leaves to test first.

points: Start with a hypothesis; test it with the minimum data needed.
MECE: no overlaps, no gaps.
Diagnostic trees ask 'why'; solution trees ask 'how'.
Use maths identities, process steps and opposites for reliable MECE splits.
Pyramid principle: answer first, then 3-ish MECE supporting arguments.
80/20 and 'so what?' on every analysis.
Seek data that could disprove you.

chapters.title: Market sizing: two fully worked Indian examples

cards.title: Why market sizing?
cards.body: Consultants and investors constantly need rough numbers fast: is this market ₹500 cr or ₹50,000 cr? Market sizing (a 'guesstimate') tests whether you can **structure** an unknown, make **sensible assumptions**, do **clean maths** and **sanity-check**. Precision matters less than logic.

cards.title: Top-down vs bottom-up
cards.body: **Top-down**: start from population or households and narrow (users × usage × price). **Bottom-up / supply-side**: count suppliers and their capacity (number of shops × sales per shop). Doing both and comparing is the best sanity check.

cards.title: A standard skeleton
cards.body: **Market value = number of users × units per user per year × price per unit.** Segment where behaviour differs (urban/rural, income bands, age), state each assumption with a one-line reason, round to easy numbers, and keep units visible.

cards.title: Example 1: smartphone screen guards
cards.body: Assume ~140 crore people; ~70 crore smartphone users (roughly half — illustrative). 60% use a screen guard → 42 crore. Replace ~1.2 times a year (breakage, new phones) → ~50 crore units. Average price ~₹150 (cheap roadside to premium tempered glass) → **≈ ₹7,500 cr a year**.

cards.title: Example 2: Bengaluru's daily milk
cards.body: Assume ~1.4 crore people (illustrative), ~4 per household → ~35 lakh households. ~1 litre per household per day (tea, coffee, curd, children) → 35 lakh L. Add ~30% for hotels, tea stalls, sweet shops → **≈ 45 lakh litres a day**.

cards.title: Sanity checks
cards.body: Check per-capita reasonableness: 45 lakh L ÷ 1.4 crore people ≈ 320 ml per person per day — plausible for a south-Indian city with heavy tea, coffee and curd use. Cross-check from supply: dairies' processing capacity, number of milk booths × litres per booth.

cards.title: Interview delivery
cards.body: Say the structure first, then numbers. Round aggressively (1.4 crore, not 1.38). Write units on every line. When the interviewer challenges an assumption, adjust calmly. End with the answer, its range, and one way to refine it with real data.

cards.q: A city has 50 lakh households; 20% own a car; each car is washed 4 times a month at ₹200. Monthly car-wash market?
cards.explain: Cars = 10 lakh; washes = 40 lakh; × ₹200 = ₹80 cr.

cards.q: Counting stores and multiplying by average sales per store is a…
cards.explain: Supply-side sizing starts from the sellers' capacity or sales.

cards.q: The best way to sanity-check a market size is to…
options: Cross-check with a second method or a per-capita figure
cards.explain: Triangulating with another approach catches unrealistic assumptions.

notes.p:
Market sizing estimates the size of a market — in units or rupees — from logic and reasonable assumptions when data is unavailable or unreliable. Real uses: a startup's TAM for investors, an FMCG firm deciding whether to launch in a new category, a consultant's quick check on whether an opportunity is worth a study. In interviews, it tests **structured thinking, numeracy and composure**.

The answer doesn't need to be 'correct'. It needs to be **defensible**: a clear structure, assumptions that a reasonable person accepts, maths without errors, and a sanity check.

points: **1. Clarify**: value or volume? Annual? Which geography? B2C only or also B2B? New sales or installed base?
**2. Choose the approach**: demand-side (population → users → usage → price) or supply-side (sellers × capacity). Use the one with better-known anchors.
**3. Segment** where behaviour differs: urban/rural, income, age, business vs consumer.
**4. Assume, with reasons**: one line each. Use round numbers.
**5. Calculate** step by step, keeping units.
**6. Sanity-check**: per-capita figure, a second method, comparison with known numbers.

**Useful anchors** (approximate): India population ~140+ crore; ~4–5 people per household nationally (smaller in metros); a large share of the population is under 30. Use 'roughly' and update with current data.

notes.h: Worked example 1: India's annual market for smartphone screen protectors (illustrative)
notes.p:
**Clarify**: retail value, India, one year, all types (plastic film and tempered glass).

**Structure**: smartphone users × % using a protector × replacements per year × average price.

**Assumptions and maths**:
Population ≈ 140 crore.
Smartphone users ≈ 70 crore (roughly half the population; many young children, some elderly and low-income people without one).
Share using a protector ≈ 60% → **42 crore** users (common in India because phones are relatively expensive and repairs costly; some premium users skip it).
Replacements ≈ 1.2 a year (cracks, scratches, new phones) → 42 × 1.2 ≈ **50 crore units**.
Average price ≈ ₹150 (₹50–100 roadside, ₹300–800 branded tempered glass; skewed to cheap) → 50 crore × ₹150 = **₹7,500 crore** a year.

**Sanity check (supply side)**: suppose ~5 lakh mobile accessory shops and kiosks, each selling ~8–10 protectors a day for ~330 days → 5 lakh × 9 × 330 ≈ 150 crore? That is three times higher — so either shop count or daily sales is too high. Revising to ~3 lakh outlets selling ~5 a day: 3 lakh × 5 × 330 ≈ **50 crore units** — consistent. Lesson: when two methods disagree, find which assumption is weak and say so.

notes.h: Worked example 2: daily milk consumption in Bengaluru (illustrative)
notes.p:
**Clarify**: litres of liquid milk per day, including milk used for curd made at home, tea and coffee; consumed in the city (households plus businesses).

**Structure**: households × litres per household + commercial demand.

**Maths**:
Population ≈ 1.4 crore (illustrative; the metro area estimate varies).
Average household size in a metro ≈ 4 → **35 lakh households**.
Consumption ≈ 1 litre per household per day: two or three cups of tea/coffee per adult (~150–200 ml milk across them), a glass for children, home-set curd common in South India. Some households use 0.5 L, some 2 L; 1 L is a reasonable average → **35 lakh litres**.
Commercial use (hotels, darshinis, tea stalls, sweet shops, offices) ≈ 30% of household demand → **~10.5 lakh litres**.
Total ≈ **45 lakh litres a day**.

**Sanity check**: 45 lakh ÷ 1.4 crore ≈ **320 ml per person per day** — plausible, and in the range of national per-capita milk availability figures reported in recent years (a little over 400 g a day nationally, with large regional variation). **Supply check**: count milk booths and dairy routes — a large state cooperative such as KMF (Nandini) is a major supplier in the city, with private dairies adding the rest.

points: **Starting to calculate before clarifying** the question (value vs volume, which geography).
**Overly precise assumptions** (1,38,56,000 people) that slow you down.
**Losing units** — mixing per day and per year, lakh and crore.
**Not segmenting** when behaviour clearly differs (rural vs urban smartphone usage).
**No sanity check**: an answer implying every Indian buys a car each year should alarm you.
**Defending a bad assumption** when challenged instead of adjusting.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Guesstimates appear in consulting, PM and many general-management interviews in India ('How many cups of tea are sold in Mumbai a day?', 'Market size of electric two-wheelers in India'). Startups present TAM/SAM/SOM to investors: **TAM** = total addressable market, **SAM** = serviceable available market (what your model and geography can reach), **SOM** = serviceable obtainable market (what you can realistically win). In jobs, quick sizing helps prioritise which opportunities deserve detailed research.

points: Clarify scope first: value/volume, time, geography, segments.
Demand-side: users × usage × price; supply-side: sellers × capacity.
Segment where behaviour differs; state one-line reasons for each assumption.
Round numbers; keep units on every line.
Sanity-check with per-capita figures and a second method.
TAM ⊃ SAM ⊃ SOM.
End with the answer, a range and how you'd refine it.

chapters.title: Profitability and market-entry frameworks (with a worked case)

cards.title: The profit tree
cards.body: **Profit = Revenue − Costs.** Revenue = Σ (volume × price) across products and channels. Costs = fixed + variable (variable = volume × unit cost). Every profitability case starts by finding **which branch moved** — and by how much — before asking why.

cards.title: Diagnose with numbers first
cards.body: Ask for (or estimate) revenue and cost over time, then split each: by product, customer segment, channel, geography. Compare with competitors: if everyone's profit fell, look **outside** (market, regulation, input prices); if only your client's fell, look **inside**.

cards.title: Worked: QSR profit drop
cards.body: A pizza chain's profit fell from ₹50 cr to ₹30 cr. Revenue rose ₹500 → ₹520 cr; costs rose ₹450 → ₹490 cr. Food cost (35%) rose ₹7 cr; other costs fell ₹7 cr.
