But **aggregator commissions** jumped from ₹25 to ₹65 cr as delivery-app orders went from 20% to 50% of sales at a 25% commission. Root cause found.

cards.title: Market-entry framework
cards.body: Should we enter? Check four things: **Market** (size, growth, profitability), **Competition** (who's there, how they'll react, barriers), **Company** (capabilities, fit, right to win), **Economics** (investment, breakeven, payback) — then **entry mode** (build, buy, partner) and risks.

cards.title: Worked: breakeven for entry
cards.body: Ice-cream brand entering a new state: fixed costs (cold chain, marketing, staff) ₹40 cr/yr; contribution 30% of net revenue → breakeven net revenue = 40 ÷ 0.3 ≈ ₹133 cr. Retailers keep ~30% → ~₹190 cr at retail ≈ **9.5% of a ₹2,000 cr market**. Is ~10% share achievable in 3 years against entrenched leaders?

cards.title: Right to win
cards.body: Market attractiveness isn't enough; ask why **you** will win. Sources: brand that travels, cost advantage, distribution you can reuse, technology, or a gap incumbents ignore. Without a right to win, an attractive market just attracts losses.

cards.title: Recommend clearly
cards.body: End every case with a recommendation, two or three reasons with numbers, risks and next steps: 'Enter, but via an acquisition of a regional player, because building cold chain alone delays breakeven to year 5.' Hedging ('it depends') without a call is the commonest way to lose a case.

cards.q: Revenue rose 4% but profit fell 40%. Where should you look first?
options: Costs — find which line grew fastest
cards.explain: With revenue up, the profit fall must come from costs (or mix); find the branch that moved.

cards.q: Fixed costs ₹24 cr, contribution margin 40%. Breakeven revenue?
If every competitor's margins fell at the same time, the most likely cause is…
options: An industry-wide factor such as input costs, demand or regulation
cards.explain: Common shocks point to external factors; client-only declines point inward.

notes.p: Two case types make up a large share of consulting interviews and real strategy work: **profitability** ('Why are profits falling and what should we do?') and **market entry** ('Should we enter this market, and how?'). Both reward the same approach: a clean structure tied to arithmetic, quick identification of what really moved, and a crisp recommendation. Frameworks are **checklists for thinking**, not scripts to recite — tailor them to the client's industry.

points: **Profit = Revenue − Costs**.
**Revenue** = volume × price, split by product, segment, channel, geography. Watch **mix shifts** (more low-margin products) as well as levels.
**Costs** = fixed (rent, salaries, depreciation) + variable (materials, commissions, freight). Check cost per unit, not just totals.
**Benchmark**: over time (when did it change?) and vs competitors (is it everyone or just us?).
**Root cause** behind the branch: market (demand, pricing pressure), competition, customer behaviour, operations, regulation.
**Solutions**: raise price, change mix, cut costs, renegotiate, change channel strategy — prioritised by impact and feasibility.

notes.p:
**Situation**: a regional pizza chain with 300 outlets saw operating profit fall from ₹50 cr to ₹30 cr in a year, despite revenue growth.

**Step 1 — split profit**: revenue ₹500 cr → ₹520 cr (+4%): orders 2.5 crore → 2.6 crore, average order value flat at ₹200. Costs ₹450 cr → ₹490 cr (+₹40 cr). The problem is costs.

**Step 2 — split costs**:
Food cost at 35% of revenue: ₹175 cr → ₹182 cr (+₹7 cr, simply volume).
Aggregator commissions: last year 20% of revenue came via delivery apps at a 25% commission: 500 × 20% × 25% = **₹25 cr**. This year 50% of revenue via apps: 520 × 50% × 25% = **₹65 cr** (+₹40 cr).
Other costs (rent, staff, utilities): ₹250 cr → ₹243 cr (−₹7 cr, small savings).
Total: 182 + 65 + 243 = ₹490 cr ✓. Profit = 520 − 490 = ₹30 cr ✓.

**Step 3 — root cause**: customers shifted from dine-in and the chain's own delivery to aggregator apps. Each order via an app earns roughly ₹50 less contribution (25% of ₹200).

**Step 4 — options**: (a) push the **own app/website** with loyalty rewards and a modest discount — every order moved back saves ~₹50 minus the discount; (b) **menu pricing** slightly higher on aggregator apps where allowed; (c) negotiate commission based on volume; (d) design delivery-only combos with higher margins.

**Recommendation**: 'Recover ₹15–20 cr within a year by shifting 15–20 percentage points of delivery orders back to our own channel through a loyalty programme, and by app-specific pricing and combos.' A quick check of option (a): moving 15% of ₹520 cr = ₹78 cr of revenue off apps saves 25% of it, about ₹19.5 cr, before the cost of the loyalty programme.

points: **Market**: size and growth, profitability, customer segments, trends, regulation.
**Competition**: concentration, leaders' shares, likely retaliation, barriers to entry (distribution, brand, licences, scale).
**Company fit and right to win**: capabilities that transfer, brand, cost position, relationships.
**Economics**: investment, fixed and variable costs, breakeven volume/share, payback, NPV.
**Entry mode**: build (greenfield, slow, full control), buy (fast, expensive, integration risk), partner/JV (shared risk and control), license/franchise (asset-light).
**Risks and mitigation**, and a staged plan (pilot city first).

notes.h: Worked case: entering a new state (illustrative)
notes.p:
A western-India ice-cream brand considers entering Tamil Nadu, where the illustrative retail market is **₹2,000 cr** a year, growing ~10%, led by two established players.

**Economics**: annual fixed costs — co-packing contract, cold-chain fleet and freezers in outlets, marketing, sales team — **₹40 cr**. Contribution margin on net revenue (after retailer margins) **30%**. Breakeven net revenue = 40 ÷ 0.30 ≈ **₹133 cr**. Retailers keep ~30% of retail price, so retail sales needed = 133 ÷ 0.7 ≈ **₹190 cr** → about **9.5% market share**.

**Judgement**: reaching ~10% share against entrenched leaders could take several years; freezer placement in outlets is the main barrier. Options: (1) build slowly, city by city (Chennai, Coimbatore), accepting losses for 3–4 years; (2) **acquire a regional brand** with existing freezers and distribution, reaching breakeven sooner; (3) partner with a dairy cooperative for distribution.

**Recommendation (one possible answer)**: enter via acquisition of a regional player if one is available at a sensible price; otherwise pilot in Chennai to test share gains before committing ₹40 cr a year state-wide.

points: **Reciting a framework** without tailoring it to the industry.
**Diving into causes before quantifying** which branch moved.
**Ignoring mix** — overall price flat can hide a shift to low-margin products.
**Treating market attractiveness as enough** — forgetting the right to win and competitor response.
**No numbers in the recommendation**.
**Forgetting implementation risks** (talent, regulation, timing).

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Consulting interviews at MBB and Big Four firms frequently include these two case types; Indian B-school case books are full of them. In real jobs, the same logic drives business reviews ('margins fell 2 points — why?') and board papers on new markets. Strategy exams test entry modes and their trade-offs (control vs speed vs risk).

points: Profit = revenue − costs; revenue = volume × price; costs = fixed + variable.
Quantify which branch moved before asking why; check mix.
Benchmark over time and against competitors (internal vs external causes).
Market entry: market, competition, company/right to win, economics, entry mode, risks.
Breakeven revenue = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin %.
Build vs buy vs partner trades control, speed and risk.
Always finish with a clear, quantified recommendation.

chapters.title: How to crack a case interview: structure, maths and synthesis

cards.title: What the interviewer is testing
cards.body: A case interview is a simulated client problem, usually ~30 minutes. Interviewers assess: **structuring** (can you break it down?), **analytics** (can you do maths and read charts?), **business judgement** (do your ideas make sense?), **synthesis** (can you land a recommendation?) and **communication** — would a client trust you?

cards.title: The flow of a case
cards.body: 1) **Listen and clarify** the objective. 2) Take a minute to **structure** — draw a tailored issue tree. 3) Walk the interviewer through it and state a **hypothesis**. 4) **Analyse** data, maths and charts they give you. 5) **Brainstorm** creatively when asked. 6) **Synthesise**: recommendation, reasons, risks, next steps.

cards.title: Interviewer-led vs candidate-led
cards.body: **Interviewer-led** (McKinsey style): the interviewer asks a series of specific questions — structure, a chart, a calculation, brainstorm. **Candidate-led** (common at BCG, Bain and others): you drive — decide what to analyse next and ask for data. Practise both.

cards.title: Case maths toolkit
cards.body: Know: percentages and growth, breakeven = fixed ÷ unit contribution, margins, simple NPV and payback, weighted averages, and quick multiplication with zeros (lakh/crore ↔ million/billion: 1 crore = 10 million; 1 lakh = 100,000). Say steps aloud, round sensibly, and **sanity-check** each result.

cards.title: Worked: case maths
cards.body: Client: a coaching institute considering a ₹6 cr new centre. Each student pays ₹1.5 lakh; variable cost ₹50,000 per student; fixed costs ₹3 cr a year. Contribution ₹1 lakh/student → breakeven **300 students** a year. At 400 students: profit ₹1 cr a year → simple payback on ₹6 cr ≈ **6 years**.

cards.title: The synthesis
cards.body: Lead with the answer: '**Recommendation:** don't open the centre now.' Then 2–3 reasons with numbers ('payback ~6 years exceeds the 3-year target; demand uncertain'), then **risks** and **next steps** ('test demand with an online batch'). Ninety seconds, top-down, no recap of everything you did.

cards.title: How to prepare
cards.body: Do 30–50 live cases with partners, not just reading. Keep a log of mistakes (missed clarifying question, maths slip, weak synthesis). Practise mental maths daily. Read business news to build intuition on Indian industries. Case books from IIM consulting clubs and books like *Case in Point* (Marc Cosentino) help.

cards.q: Fixed costs ₹2 cr; price ₹500; variable cost ₹300 per unit. Breakeven volume?
cards.explain: Contribution = ₹200/unit; ₹2 cr ÷ ₹200 = 1,00,000 units.

cards.q: The best way to open your final synthesis is…
cards.explain: Top-down: answer first, then reasons.

cards.q: ₹50 crore is equal to…
cards.explain: 1 crore = 10 million, so 50 crore = 500 million rupees.

notes.p: Case interviews are the gateway to consulting jobs and increasingly to strategy, PM and general-management roles. They are not tests of business trivia; they are **simulations of how you think** with a client in the room. A good case performance looks like a calm, structured conversation: you clarify, structure, quantify, judge and conclude. These skills are learnable, and practice volume matters more than raw talent.

notes.h: Step by step through a case
points: **1. Listen and take notes**: client, situation, objective, constraints, numbers.
**2. Clarify**: the objective and metric ('grow profit or revenue?'), time frame, geography, any constraints. Two or three questions, not ten.
**3. Structure**: ask for a minute; draw a MECE tree tailored to the problem — not a generic framework. Present it top-down and number the buckets.
**4. Hypothesis and prioritise**: 'I suspect costs, because revenue grew. I'd start there.'
**5. Analyse**: interpret exhibits (state the key insight first: 'This chart shows our share falling only in tier-2 cities'), do maths aloud, and state the 'so what'.
**6. Brainstorm**: give structured ideas (internal vs external; short- vs long-term), not a random list.
**7. Synthesise**: recommendation → reasons with numbers → risks → next steps.

notes.p:
**Prompt**: 'A test-prep company wants to open a new centre in Indore. Should it?'

**Clarify**: objective — profitable expansion with payback under 3 years. Investment ₹6 cr (fit-out, equipment, launch marketing).

**Structure**: (1) Demand — students who might enrol, competition, price; (2) Economics — contribution, fixed costs, breakeven, payback; (3) Capability — faculty availability, brand strength in that city; (4) Risks.

**Maths**: fee ₹1.5 lakh per student; variable cost (materials, variable faculty pay, payment fees) ₹50,000 → **contribution ₹1 lakh**. Fixed costs (rent, core faculty, admin) ₹3 cr a year → **breakeven 300 students**. Interviewer says realistic enrolment is 350–450 by year 2. At 400: profit = 400 × 1 lakh − 3 cr = **₹1 cr a year** → payback on ₹6 cr ≈ **6 years** (ignoring ramp-up, which makes it worse).

**Judgement**: even at 450 students (profit ₹1.5 cr), payback is 4 years — above the 3-year hurdle. Could a hybrid model (smaller centre + online classes) cut fixed costs to ₹2 cr? Then at 400 students profit = ₹2 cr; with a smaller ₹4 cr investment, payback ≈ 2 years.

**Synthesis**: 'I recommend not opening a full-scale centre now. Payback is ~6 years against a 3-year target. Instead, launch a hybrid centre with ~₹4 cr investment and ₹2 cr fixed costs, which pays back in about 2 years at expected enrolment. Key risk: competition from established local institutes; next step: test demand with an online batch for Indore students.'

**Maths tips**: break numbers apart (18 × 45 = 18 × 50 − 18 × 5 = 900 − 90 = 810); use powers of ten and keep track of zeros; convert units early (1 lakh = 10⁵; 1 crore = 10⁷; ₹1,000 crore = ₹10 billion); approximate when allowed ('roughly 33%'); always state units in answers.

**Exhibits**: read the title, axes, units and footnotes first; find the one big insight (biggest change, outlier, trend); connect it to your hypothesis; then mention one secondary observation. Don't narrate every bar.

points: **Generic frameworks** recited without tailoring (Porter's five forces for a cost-cutting case).
**Silent thinking**: the interviewer can't credit reasoning they don't hear.
**Maths errors from rushing** — slow down, write numbers neatly, sanity-check.
**Not using the data given** or ignoring the interviewer's hints.
**Rambling synthesis** that recaps the process instead of answering.
**Losing composure** after a mistake — acknowledge it, fix it, move on; recovery is noted favourably.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Consulting recruitment at Indian B-schools (MBB, Big Four strategy arms, Accenture Strategy and others) typically runs several case rounds plus a fit/behavioural interview ('Why consulting?', 'Tell me about a time you led a team'). Many corporate strategy, PM and founder's-office roles also use cases. On the job, the same flow — structure, hypothesis, analysis, synthesis — runs every client engagement and every steering-committee deck.

points: Tested: structure, analytics, judgement, synthesis, communication.
Flow: clarify → structure → hypothesis → analyse → brainstorm → synthesise.
Tailor MECE structures; don't recite frameworks.
Maths: say steps aloud, keep units, sanity-check; 1 crore = 10 million.
Exhibits: title and units first, then the one big insight and its 'so what'.
Synthesis: answer → 2–3 numbered reasons → risks → next steps.
Preparation: 30–50 live cases, a mistake log, daily mental maths.

chapters.title: International expansion and global strategy

cards.title: Distance still matters
cards.body: Pankaj Ghemawat's HBR article 'Distance Still Matters' (2001) argued that firms overestimate foreign market size and underestimate the **distance** between home and host. Country attractiveness must be adjusted for how far away a market really is — not just in kilometres.

cards.title: CAGE framework
cards.body: Four kinds of distance: **Cultural** (language, religion, norms, tastes), **Administrative** (colonial ties, trade agreements, laws, currency), **Geographic** (physical distance, time zones, climate, infrastructure), **Economic** (income levels, costs, resources). Different industries are sensitive to different distances.

cards.title: Global integration vs local responsiveness
cards.body: Bartlett and Ghoshal's typology: **International** (export home model), **Multidomestic** (adapt heavily per country), **Global** (standardise for scale), **Transnational** (both scale and local adaptation — hard but powerful). The choice depends on cost pressure vs need for local adaptation.

cards.title: Entry modes
cards.body: From low to high commitment and control: **exporting** → **licensing/franchising** → **joint venture or strategic alliance** → **wholly owned subsidiary** (via acquisition or greenfield). More control means more risk and capital; JVs are sometimes required or wise where local knowledge and relationships matter.

cards.title: Case: Indian IT goes global
cards.body: Indian IT services firms grew by serving US and UK clients. CAGE explains part of it: **low cultural/administrative distance** for English-speaking, common-law markets; **time-zone difference** turned into a 24-hour delivery advantage; and large **economic distance** (wage differences) was the core value proposition.

cards.title: Case: Walmart in Germany
cards.body: Walmart entered Germany in the late 1990s through acquisitions and exited in 2006 after years of losses. Commonly cited reasons: an entrenched, efficient discount sector (Aldi, Lidl), regulatory constraints, and practices that didn't translate culturally. Big home-market strength didn't travel.

cards.title: Adapt, aggregate, arbitrage
cards.body: Ghemawat's AAA strategies: **Adaptation** (tailor to local differences — McDonald's India menu with no beef), **Aggregation** (exploit similarities across regions for scale), **Arbitrage** (exploit differences — cheaper labour, resources). Most firms emphasise one or two.

cards.q: Which is an 'administrative' distance in CAGE?
options: Absence of a trade agreement and different legal systems
cards.explain: Administrative distance covers political, legal and institutional differences, including trade agreements.

cards.q: A firm that wants local partners' market knowledge while sharing risk most likely chooses…
cards.explain: JVs share risk and give access to local knowledge and relationships, at the cost of shared control.

cards.q: Indian IT firms using offshore delivery to exploit wage differences is mainly which AAA strategy?
cards.explain: Arbitrage exploits differences between countries, such as labour costs.

notes.p:
Going global is one of the biggest strategic bets a company makes. The pull is obvious: new customers, scale, talent, diversification. The push-back is subtler: foreign markets are **distant** in culture, institutions, geography and economics, and incumbents there have home advantages. Many international expansions disappoint because managers judge markets by size alone.

Indian companies have expanded abroad both organically and through acquisitions — Tata (JLR, Tetley, Corus), Bharti Airtel (Africa), Hindalco (Novelis), Sun Pharma, the IT services firms — while global firms have learnt (sometimes painfully) to adapt to India.

points: **Cultural**: language, ethnicity, religion, social norms, tastes. Matters most for products with high linguistic or cultural content — food, media, retail.
**Administrative/political**: colonial links, common currency or trade blocs, legal systems, corruption, government policies. Matters for regulated sectors and those seen as strategic.
**Geographic**: physical distance, borders, time zones, climate, transport and communication links. Matters for heavy, perishable or service-intensive products.
**Economic**: differences in income, labour costs, resources, infrastructure. Can be a barrier (premium product in a low-income market) or an opportunity (arbitrage).
Use CAGE to **discount** raw market size: a large market at high distance may be worth less than a smaller, closer one.

notes.p: **Integration–responsiveness grid** (Prahalad and Doz; Bartlett and Ghoshal's *Managing Across Borders*, 1989):
points: **International**: home-developed products sold abroad with little change; works when local pressures and cost pressures are low.
**Multidomestic**: country units adapt heavily — common in food and consumer goods.
**Global**: standardised products to maximise scale — semiconductors, aircraft components.

**Transnational**: global efficiency, local responsiveness and worldwide learning at once — HUL-Unilever-style knowledge flows (e.g. small sachet packaging innovations spreading across emerging markets) are often cited.
**AAA** (Ghemawat, 2007): Adaptation, Aggregation, Arbitrage — choose emphasis.

notes.h: Entry modes and the Uppsala model
notes.p:
**Entry modes**, increasing in commitment, control and risk: indirect/direct **exporting**; **licensing** (sell rights to IP); **franchising** (sell a business format — e.g. global QSR brands in India run by Indian franchisees such as Jubilant FoodWorks for Domino's and Westlife for McDonald's in the west and south); **contract manufacturing**; **joint ventures** (Maruti Suzuki began as a JV between the Government of India and Suzuki; many insurance companies in India are JVs with foreign partners due to historical FDI caps); **wholly owned subsidiaries** via **acquisition** (fast, buys local presence) or **greenfield** (full control, slow).

The **Uppsala model** (Johanson and Vahlne, 1977) observed that firms often internationalise **incrementally** — first to psychically close markets, with low-commitment modes, increasing commitment as they learn. 'Born-global' startups, especially in software, challenge this pattern by selling worldwide from day one (Freshworks and Zoho are Indian SaaS examples with large international customer bases).

An Indian packaged-snacks company compares two markets.

**Market A — the UAE**: smaller population, but large Indian diaspora (low cultural distance for core products), good air and sea links (low geographic distance), simple trade relations (an India–UAE trade agreement, CEPA, took effect in 2022), high incomes (economic distance favourable for premium pricing).

**Market B — Brazil**: much larger population but high cultural distance (tastes, Portuguese language), high geographic distance (shipping, time zones), different regulation and labelling rules, and established local and global snack players.

Scoring each CAGE dimension 1 (close) to 5 (far): A = 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = **7**; B = 5 + 4 + 5 + 3 = **17**. Even if Brazil's snack market is many times larger, the company's realistic share and margins there are likely far lower. Sensible sequence: export to the UAE via distributors → learn → expand to other diaspora-heavy markets (UK, US) → consider distant markets later via partnership or acquisition.

points: **Market-size fixation** ignoring distance and competition.
**Copy-paste**: assuming the home playbook works abroad (Walmart in Germany; several global retailers' early struggles in India).
**Over-adaptation** that destroys scale economies.
**Underestimating regulation and politics** — e.g. foreign ride-hailing and e-commerce firms facing local rules; Uber sold its China business to Didi in 2016 after an expensive battle.
**Overpaying for 'transformational' cross-border acquisitions** without integration capacity.
**Ignoring currency risk** and repatriation constraints.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Strategy exams ask you to apply CAGE or the integration–responsiveness grid to a company, and to compare entry modes. Consulting cases ask: 'Should an Indian EV maker enter Southeast Asia?' — answer with attractiveness, CAGE distance, right to win, economics and entry mode. In jobs, international business teams build country-prioritisation scorecards and partner-selection criteria.

points: Distance still matters (Ghemawat, 2001): adjust market size for distance.
CAGE: Cultural, Administrative, Geographic, Economic.
Strategies: international, multidomestic, global, transnational.
AAA: Adaptation, Aggregation, Arbitrage.
Entry modes: export → license/franchise → JV/alliance → wholly owned (acquisition or greenfield).
Uppsala: incremental internationalisation; born-globals challenge it.
Cases: Indian IT (arbitrage), Walmart Germany (failed transfer), McDonald's India (adaptation).

chapters.title: Leading change: Kotter's 8 steps and overcoming resistance

cards.title: Why change efforts fail
cards.body: John Kotter's HBR article 'Leading Change: Why Transformation Efforts Fail' (1995) and book *Leading Change* (1996) argued that most transformations fail not for lack of strategy but from predictable leadership mistakes — not enough urgency, weak coalitions, under-communicated visions, and declaring victory too soon.

cards.title: Kotter's 8 steps (1–4)
cards.body: 1) **Establish a sense of urgency** — make the cost of standing still vivid. 2) **Create a guiding coalition** with enough power and credibility. 3) **Develop a vision and strategy**. 4) **Communicate the change vision** — constantly, through words and leaders' behaviour.

cards.title: Kotter's 8 steps (5–8)
cards.body: 5) **Empower broad-based action** — remove obstacles, systems and people blocking change. 6) **Generate short-term wins** — visible, early proof it works. 7) **Consolidate gains and produce more change** — don't declare victory early. 8) **Anchor new approaches in the culture** — through hiring, promotion and stories.

cards.title: Why people resist
cards.body: Resistance is rational from the inside: fear of losing status, skills becoming obsolete, more work, uncertainty, distrust of leaders, or genuine disagreement. Kotter and Schlesinger (HBR, 1979) listed responses: education, participation, facilitation and support, negotiation, manipulation/co-optation, and coercion — each with costs.

cards.title: Lewin's three stages
cards.body: Kurt Lewin's classic model: **Unfreeze** (challenge the status quo), **Change** (move to new behaviours), **Refreeze** (stabilise them). Simple but useful: most failures happen because organisations skip unfreezing or never refreeze.

cards.title: Case: Microsoft under Satya Nadella
cards.body: From 2014, Nadella reframed Microsoft's culture from 'know-it-all' to 'learn-it-all' (drawing on Carol Dweck's growth mindset), shifted strategy to cloud and cross-platform products, and modelled new behaviours himself. Urgency (missed mobile), clear vision (cloud-first) and consistent leadership signals fit Kotter's logic.

cards.title: The change maths
cards.body: Change success ≈ quality of the idea × acceptance by people. A brilliant plan that 30% of staff adopt delivers less than a decent plan that 90% adopt. Budget as much effort for communication, training and incentives as for the design itself.

cards.q: In Kotter's model, which step comes right after creating a sense of urgency?
cards.explain: Step 2 is forming a powerful guiding coalition.

cards.q: Declaring victory after the first successful pilot mostly violates which Kotter step?
options: Consolidate gains and produce more change
cards.explain: Step 7 warns against declaring victory too soon; momentum must be used to drive deeper change.

cards.q: Involving resisters in designing the change is an example of…
cards.explain: Participation builds commitment and uses resisters' knowledge, though it takes time.

notes.p:
Strategy decides **where** to go; change leadership gets **people** there. Most organisational transformations — digital, cost, cultural, post-merger — fall short of their goals; Kotter's work and later consulting surveys repeatedly report high failure rates (often quoted around 'most' or 'two-thirds', though exact figures are debated). The reasons are rarely technical. People don't see why they should change, don't trust the leaders driving it, or slip back to old habits once attention moves on.

Change management is therefore a core general-management skill — whether you're rolling out a new ERP in a factory, merging two sales teams, or shifting a bank's culture toward digital.

points: **1. Establish a sense of urgency**: share hard data on threats and opportunities; make the status quo feel riskier than change.
**2. Create the guiding coalition**: a team with position power, expertise, credibility and leadership — not just the HR department.
**3. Develop a vision and strategy**: a picture of the future that can be explained in five minutes.
**4. Communicate the change vision**: repeatedly, through many channels; leaders must 'walk the talk'.
**5. Empower broad-based action**: remove structural barriers, change systems (incentives, approvals), deal with blockers.
**6. Generate short-term wins**: plan visible improvements in 6–18 months; reward the people involved.
**7. Consolidate gains and produce more change**: use credibility from wins to tackle bigger systems and policies.
**8. Anchor new approaches in the culture**: show the link between new behaviours and success; build it into hiring, promotion and succession.
Kotter later (*Accelerate*, 2014) proposed a more networked version with a 'volunteer army' — but the classic eight steps remain the standard teaching model.

notes.p: Kotter and Schlesinger's 'Choosing Strategies for Change' (HBR, 1979) identified four common reasons for resistance — **parochial self-interest**, **misunderstanding and lack of trust**, **different assessments** of the situation, and **low tolerance for change** — and matched them with approaches:
points: **Education and communication** — when resistance comes from misinformation.
**Participation and involvement** — when initiators lack information or need commitment.
**Facilitation and support** — training, counselling, time off when fear and anxiety drive resistance.
**Negotiation and agreement** — when a group clearly loses (e.g. unions).
**Manipulation and co-optation** — risky; backfires if discovered.
**Explicit and implicit coercion** — fast but breeds resentment; used when speed is essential.
Also useful: the **change curve** (shock, denial, frustration, experimentation, acceptance), adapted from Kübler-Ross's work on grief.

notes.h: Worked example: digitising a public-sector bank's branch processes (illustrative)
notes.p:
**Context**: a large bank wants all loan applications processed through a new digital workflow, cutting turnaround from 15 days to 3.

**Urgency**: show data — fintech lenders approve small loans in hours; the bank's market share in personal loans has been falling.
**Coalition**: the MD, retail head, CIO, two respected zonal managers and a union representative.
**Vision**: 'Every customer gets a loan decision in 3 days, every branch officer spends more time selling than on paperwork.'
**Communication**: town halls, branch visits, a weekly dashboard of turnaround by zone.
**Empowerment**: retrain 5,000 staff; remove the requirement for physical file sign-offs; change incentives to reward turnaround and quality.
**Short-term wins**: pilot in 50 branches; turnaround falls to 4 days within three months — publicise and reward the pilot teams.
**Consolidate**: roll out zone by zone; fix IT issues found in pilots; extend to MSME loans.
**Anchor**: include digital adoption in promotion criteria; new joiners trained only on the new system.

**Resistance map**: older officers fear the technology (facilitation, buddy training); some managers lose control over approvals (participation in redesign, new roles); union concerns about job losses (negotiation: commitment to redeploy, not retrench).

points: **Announcing change by email** and assuming it's done.
**Coalition of the junior**: no senior power behind the change.
**Vision as a slogan** with no concrete picture of daily work.
**Leaders' behaviour contradicting the message** (preaching frugality while upgrading their own offices).
**No short-term wins**, so sceptics win the argument.
**Declaring victory too soon** — after the system goes live, before behaviours stick.
**Treating resisters as enemies** rather than sources of information.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: OB and strategy exams ask you to apply Kotter or Lewin to a case. Interviews ask behavioural questions: 'Tell me about a time you led change or persuaded a resistant team.' Use the STAR format and mention urgency, allies, quick wins. Consultants and managers use change plans in every transformation — post-merger integration, ERP rollouts, cost programmes.

points: Kotter (1995/1996): most transformations fail from predictable leadership mistakes.
Eight steps: urgency → coalition → vision → communicate → empower → short-term wins → consolidate → anchor in culture.
Lewin: unfreeze → change → refreeze.
Resistance reasons: self-interest, mistrust, different assessments, low tolerance for change.
Responses: education, participation, support, negotiation, co-optation, coercion (Kotter & Schlesinger, 1979).
Leaders' behaviour communicates more than speeches.
Don't declare victory too soon; anchor change in hiring and promotion.

chapters.title: Family businesses in India: succession and governance

cards.title: Family firms run India
cards.body: A large share of India's listed companies and most private businesses are family-controlled — from giant groups (Tata, Reliance, Aditya Birla, Mahindra, Bajaj, Godrej, Murugappa) to lakhs of MSMEs. Their strengths: long-term view, fast decisions, trust. Their risks: succession fights, nepotism, and mixing family and business.

cards.title: The three-circle model
cards.body: Tagiuri and Davis (1982) mapped three overlapping systems: **Family**, **Ownership**, **Business (management)**. A person can be in one, two or all three — e.g. a family member who owns shares but doesn't work in the firm. Most conflicts come from confusing the roles, such as treating a family member as an employee who can't be fired.

cards.title: Succession: the hardest decision
cards.body: Questions: who leads next — a family member or a professional CEO? How are they prepared (outside experience, rotations, mentoring)? When does the founder truly step back? How is ownership divided, and is management separated from ownership? Plans should start a decade early, not after a crisis.

cards.title: Cases: splits and transitions
cards.body: After Dhirubhai Ambani's death in 2002, a public dispute between his sons led to the **2005 split of Reliance**. In 2024, the **Godrej** family agreed an amicable realignment into two groups. Tata Sons' removal of Cyrus Mistry as chairman in 2016 led to a long legal battle, decided in Tata Sons' favour by the Supreme Court in 2021.

cards.title: Governance tools
cards.body: **Family constitution** (values, rules for joining the business, share transfers, dispute resolution), **family council** (forum for family issues), **board with independent directors** (business decisions), **family office** (manages wealth outside the business), **employment policies** (qualifications, outside experience for family members).

cards.title: Worked: ownership fragmentation
cards.body: Founder owns 100%. Three children: 33.3% each. Each has three children: nine cousins at **11.1%**. Next generation, again three each: 27 owners at **3.7%**. A ₹30 cr dividend once fed 3 households at ₹10 cr; now it's ~₹1.1 cr each — and many owners don't work in the firm. Pressure for dividends, exits and splits rises.

cards.title: Professionalise without losing the soul
cards.body: Successful family groups often keep family members as **stewards and owners** while hiring professional managers, using merit-based rules for family employment, and preserving values — Tata's trusts-led ownership and long-serving professional leaders are a frequently cited model, Infosys's founders a non-family contrast.

cards.q: In the three-circle model, a family member who owns shares but doesn't work in the firm sits in…
cards.explain: They're in the family and ownership circles but not the business (management) circle.

cards.q: A written document setting rules for family members joining the business and selling shares is a…
cards.explain: A family constitution codifies values, rules and dispute processes.

cards.q: Ownership split equally among 4 children, each later splitting equally among 4 children. Each grandchild owns about…

notes.p:
Family businesses combine two systems with different logics. **Families** run on love, equality and belonging; **businesses** run on merit, performance and hard trade-offs. When they reinforce each other, the result can be extraordinary longevity and patient capital. When they collide — over who leads, who gets paid, who owns what — they can destroy both the firm and the family.

In India, family businesses dominate the corporate landscape, from century-old groups to first-generation entrepreneurs. Studies of listed Indian companies consistently find promoter families controlling a large share of them. An old proverb found in many cultures — 'shirtsleeves to shirtsleeves in three generations' — captures the risk: wealth and businesses often fail to survive beyond the third generation.

notes.h: The framework: three circles and the generational shift
notes.p:
**Three-circle model** (Renato Tagiuri and John Davis, 1982): Family, Ownership and Business overlap to create seven positions. Each position has legitimate but different interests — a non-working owner wants dividends; a working family manager wants reinvestment and salary; a non-family executive wants merit-based promotion.

**Generational stages** (described by John Ward, Kelin Gersick and others):
points: **Controlling owner (founder stage)**: one decision-maker, informal governance, speed.
**Sibling partnership**: a few siblings share ownership and management; need rules for decisions and roles.
**Cousin consortium**: many owners, most not working in the firm; needs formal governance, liquidity options and professional management.
Each stage needs different governance; using founder-stage informality in a cousin consortium invites conflict.

notes.h: Worked example: ownership fragmentation and its consequences (illustrative)
notes.p:
**Generation 1**: founder owns 100% of a company that pays ₹30 cr a year in dividends.
**Generation 2**: three children, 33.3% each → ₹10 cr dividend each. All three work in the business.
**Generation 3**: each has three children → **nine cousins at 11.1%** → ₹3.3 cr each. Perhaps four work in the business.
**Generation 4**: three children each again → **27 owners at 3.7%** → about ₹1.1 cr each. Maybe five work in the business.

Consequences: non-working owners press for higher dividends or the right to sell; working owners want reinvestment; branches compare each other's perks; decisions slow down. Solutions families adopt: a **share buyback or liquidity window** for those who want out; **holding companies per branch**; **dividend policy** written into the family constitution; **separation of businesses** among branches (as in several Indian group realignments); and a professional board that makes business decisions on merit.

**Succession planning** should start early: define criteria for leadership; require family successors to gain **outside work experience**; rotate them through roles with real accountability; consider **professional CEOs** with family as chair or board members; and set a clear transition timeline for the founder.

**Governance architecture**:
points: **Family constitution / charter**: values, mission, rules on employment, share ownership and transfers, conflict resolution, exit.
**Family assembly and family council**: forums for communication and education of the wider family.
**Board of directors with independent directors**: business oversight; SEBI's listing rules already require independent directors for listed firms.

**Family office and trusts**: separate family wealth and philanthropy from operating businesses. Tata Sons is majority-owned by philanthropic Tata Trusts — an unusual structure that has helped keep the group together.
**Clear compensation**: family members paid market salaries for jobs, dividends for ownership — not mixed.

notes.p:
**Reliance**: Dhirubhai Ambani died in 2002; disagreements between his sons Mukesh and Anil became public and the group was divided in 2005 with mediation by their mother, Kokilaben. The brothers' subsequent paths diverged sharply.
**Godrej**: in 2024, the Godrej family announced an amicable realignment, splitting the group between two branches through a family settlement — often cited as an orderly way to resolve diverging interests.
**Tata**: the 2016 removal of Cyrus Mistry as Tata Sons chairman triggered a prolonged dispute; the Supreme Court ruled in favour of Tata Sons in 2021. It highlighted tensions between trusts, minority shareholders and professional leadership.
**Successful transitions**: many groups — for example Mahindra and Marico — have moved toward professional CEOs with family members in board or chair roles, showing ways to separate ownership from management.

points: **No written succession plan** — or a founder who never lets go.
**Nepotism**: appointing unqualified family members, which drives away professional talent.
**Equal ≠ fair**: giving every child equal management roles regardless of ability.
**Mixing money**: family expenses run through the company; related-party transactions that hurt minority shareholders.
**Avoiding hard conversations** until a death or dispute forces them.
**Ignoring in-laws and next generation** in communication.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Many Indian MBA graduates join or return to family businesses, or advise them as consultants, bankers and wealth managers. Exams ask about the three-circle model, succession and governance mechanisms. Interviews at family-owned groups probe how you would work with promoters. Private bankers and PE investors evaluate promoter quality and succession as core risks before investing.

points: Family firms dominate Indian business; strengths: long-term view, trust; risks: succession, nepotism.
Three-circle model (Tagiuri & Davis, 1982): family, ownership, business.
Stages: controlling owner → sibling partnership → cousin consortium.
Ownership fragments geometrically across generations; plan liquidity and dividends.
Governance: family constitution, family council, independent board, family office.
Separate ownership from management; pay salaries for jobs, dividends for ownership.
Cases: Reliance 2005 split, Godrej 2024 realignment, Tata–Mistry dispute.

chapters.title: Sustainability as strategy

cards.title: From CSR to strategy
cards.body: Old view: sustainability is philanthropy or compliance — a cost. Strategic view: environmental and social issues reshape **costs, risks, demand and regulation**, so they belong in core strategy. Porter and Kramer's 'Creating Shared Value' (HBR, 2011) argued firms can create economic value by solving social problems.

cards.title: Three lenses
cards.body: **Triple bottom line** (John Elkington, 1994): people, planet, profit. **ESG**: environmental, social, governance factors investors use to assess risk. **Materiality**: focus on issues that significantly affect the business and stakeholders — water for a beverage maker, data privacy for a bank, safety for a miner.

cards.title: Where value comes from
cards.body: **Cost**: energy and resource efficiency. **Revenue**: products for green and inclusive markets (EVs, solar, efficient appliances). **Risk**: climate exposure, regulation, supply-chain disruption. **Capital**: access to green finance and ESG-focused investors. **Talent and brand**: many employees and customers prefer responsible firms.

cards.title: Worked: rooftop solar payback
cards.body: Factory installs 1 MW of rooftop solar for ~₹4 cr (illustrative). It generates ~14 lakh kWh a year, replacing grid power at ₹8/kWh → **savings ≈ ₹1.12 cr a year** → simple payback **~3.6 years**. At ~0.7 tonnes CO₂ per MWh of grid power, it avoids **~980 tonnes CO₂ a year**.

cards.title: India's rules
cards.body: Companies Act 2013, **Section 135**: companies above set thresholds must spend **2% of average net profits** on CSR. SEBI's **Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR)** is mandatory for the top 1,000 listed companies by market cap, with assurance of core metrics being phased in for the largest.

cards.title: Cases
cards.body: **Unilever's** Sustainable Living Plan (2010) under Paul Polman tied brands to social purpose. **ITC's e-Choupal** (2000) used internet kiosks to give farmers price information while improving ITC's procurement. **Tata Steel** and others face carbon costs as the EU's CBAM moves into its definitive phase from 2026 — making emissions a trade issue.

cards.title: Beware greenwashing
cards.body: Claims without evidence — vague 'eco-friendly' labels, offsets of doubtful quality, net-zero targets with no interim plan — create legal and reputational risk. Credible strategy has **measured baselines, science-based targets, capex behind them, and independent assurance**.

cards.q: Under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, qualifying companies must spend on CSR…
options: 2% of average net profits of the preceding three years
Whatever the board decides, no minimum
cards.explain: The law specifies 2% of the average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years.

cards.q: A ₹2 cr energy-efficiency project saves ₹50 lakh a year. Simple payback?
cards.explain: ₹2 cr ÷ ₹0.5 cr a year = 4 years.

cards.q: 'Creating Shared Value' (2011) was proposed by…
cards.explain: Michael Porter and Mark Kramer argued firms can create economic value by addressing societal needs.

notes.p:
For decades, many firms treated social and environmental issues as **outside** strategy — handled by a CSR department, a donation, a glossy report. That view has weakened for practical reasons: energy and water costs, climate risks to assets and supply chains, carbon regulation, investor scrutiny, and changing customer and employee preferences now hit the P&L directly. **Sustainability as strategy** means asking which environmental and social issues are **material** to your business and turning them into sources of cost advantage, growth, resilience and trust.

Milton Friedman's famous 1970 essay argued the social responsibility of business is to increase profits within the rules. Shared-value thinkers reply that, increasingly, long-run profits **depend** on handling social and environmental issues well. The debate is less about whether to care than about which issues, how much, and how to measure.

points: **Triple bottom line** (Elkington, 1994): measure people and planet alongside profit. Elkington himself later called for the concept to be rethought because it had become an accounting exercise.
**Creating Shared Value** (Porter & Kramer, 2011): reconceive products and markets, redefine productivity in the value chain, and build local clusters.
**ESG**: environmental (emissions, water, waste), social (labour, safety, community, data privacy), governance (board independence, ethics, related-party dealings). Used by investors to assess risk.
**Materiality assessment**: map issues by importance to stakeholders and impact on the business; focus on the top-right quadrant.
**Emissions scopes** (GHG Protocol): Scope 1 (direct), Scope 2 (purchased electricity), Scope 3 (value chain — often the largest).
**Science-based targets**: emissions goals aligned with climate science, with interim milestones.

notes.h: Worked example: the business case for rooftop solar (illustrative)
notes.p:
A mid-sized auto-components plant in Pune evaluates a **1 MW rooftop solar** system.

**Cost**: about ₹4 cr installed (illustrative; prices vary).
**Generation**: in much of India, solar produces roughly 1,400 kWh per kW of capacity a year → 1,000 kW × 1,400 = **14 lakh kWh**.
**Savings**: displacing grid power at an industrial tariff of ₹8/kWh → 14,00,000 × 8 = **₹1.12 cr a year**. O&M ~₹5 lakh a year → net ~₹1.07 cr.
**Payback** = 4 ÷ 1.07 ≈ **3.7 years**; panels typically last 25 years, so lifetime savings are large even after degradation and inverter replacement.
**Emissions**: India's grid emits roughly 0.7 tonnes CO₂ per MWh → 1,400 MWh × 0.7 ≈ **980 tonnes of CO₂ avoided a year** — directly reducing Scope 2 emissions that the plant's European car-maker customers increasingly ask suppliers to report.

This is sustainability as strategy: lower cost, lower risk from tariff increases, and a stronger position with customers who score suppliers on emissions.

points: **CSR law**: Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 — companies with net worth ≥ ₹500 cr, turnover ≥ ₹1,000 cr or net profit ≥ ₹5 cr must spend 2% of average net profits (of the previous three years) on CSR activities in Schedule VII areas.

**BRSR**: SEBI replaced the older Business Responsibility Report with the BRSR, mandatory for the top 1,000 listed companies from FY2022–23; BRSR Core metrics with reasonable assurance are being phased in for the largest companies and extended to value chains.
**Climate goals**: India announced a net-zero target for 2070 at COP26 (2021) and has large renewable-energy capacity goals.
**Carbon markets**: the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (2023) is setting up a domestic compliance carbon market.
**Trade**: the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) affects exporters of steel, aluminium, cement and fertilisers to Europe.

**Cases**: ITC's e-Choupal and its focus on agri-supply chains; Mahindra's early work on internal carbon pricing; Tata Power and Adani Green in renewables; Unilever's Sustainable Living Plan globally; Patagonia's activist model.
**Greenwashing**: unsupported claims; regulators (e.g. in the EU, UK and India's advertising standards bodies) are tightening rules.
**Treating CSR spending as strategy**: a donation unrelated to the business rarely builds advantage.
**Targets without capex**: net-zero pledges with no investment plan or interim milestones.
**Ignoring Scope 3**: most emissions for many firms sit in suppliers and product use.
**Chasing ratings** rather than material issues.
**Short payback obsession**: rejecting 5–7 year projects that protect the business for decades.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Consulting firms run large sustainability practices (decarbonisation roadmaps, ESG due diligence). Banks and funds have ESG analysts. Corporate strategy roles assess CBAM exposure or green-product opportunities. Interview prompts: 'How should an Indian steelmaker respond to CBAM?', 'Build a business case for EV fleet conversion.' Exams test CSR law, triple bottom line, shared value, and ESG versus CSR.

points: Sustainability is strategic when it affects cost, revenue, risk, capital and talent.
Frameworks: triple bottom line (Elkington), shared value (Porter & Kramer, 2011), ESG, materiality.
Emissions: Scope 1 direct, Scope 2 purchased energy, Scope 3 value chain.
India: CSR 2% of average net profits (Sec 135); SEBI BRSR for top 1,000 listed companies.
Net zero 2070 target; domestic carbon market; EU CBAM affects exporters.
Build business cases: payback, risk reduction, customer requirements.
Avoid greenwashing: baselines, targets, capex, assurance.
